title: Mosaic
content: True to its name, Mosaic brings together several concepts—including content, design and technical infrastructure—to deliver a unified website experience that is truly greater than the sum of its individual parts.
Don't move your content where it does not belong.
Compose content from remote data sources which
are pulled at runtime by our content aggregator.
Visualize your content with your own theme, layouts and components or use the Mosaic Design
Extend the existing code and add your own content source types through our simple plugin
Publish your content through Server Side Rendering (SSR) or generate a snapshot of your content
and serve it as a Statically Generated Site (SGS).
Creating a website has never been so easy!

title: Aliases
content:
Aliases are virtual 'symlinks' of pages, allowing one page to take on one or more other routes.
This is not the same as copying the page, it is a primitive filesystem link which is resolved by Mosaic.
Use Cases
Aliases are great for linking to an old route if you've moved a page to a new place.
They can also be used to create short hand links to pages or to 'clone' a copy of a page into
another section of the site where it may be relevant.
Example
This is the frontmatter for this page:
---
title: Aliases
layout: DetailTechnical
aliases:
  - /mosaic/example/aliases
Try accessing this page from 
/mosaic/example/aliases

title: Fragments
content: Fragments, also known as content fragments, are powerful tools that allow you to incorporate content from other pages into your documentation.
By creating an MDX file and using the
, you can easily render the fragment in another file, providing modularity and reusability to your content.
Fragments offer various use cases, such as:
: Use fragments to maintain consistent content across multiple pages.
For instance, if you have a table or a tile that appears on multiple pages, you can create a fragment for it and include it in all relevant files.
This ensures that any updates made to the fragment automatically reflect across the entire documentation.
: Fragments enable the creation of reusable components or sections.
You can define a complex or commonly used section once and then include it in multiple pages as needed.
This approach saves time and effort, as you only need to update the fragment file to propagate changes throughout your documentation.
: With fragments, you can break down your documentation into smaller, manageable pieces.
Each fragment represents a specific topic or section, allowing you to organize and structure your content more efficiently.
This modular approach simplifies maintenance and makes it easier to navigate and update your documentation.

In Mosaic, each source has it's own filesystem which are then merged together to form a union of all source filesystems.
It is in this union filesystem that tags are applied and not to the individual source filesystem that the tag was defined on.
Tags are slower to apply than refs.
Multiple sources need to run and update before tagged data

title: Publish a site to AWS
content:
Publish a site to AWS using S3 snapshots.
Step 1: Create a Github repository
> git init
> git remote add origin git@github.com:username/my-sample-site.git
> git add .
> git commit -m "initial commit"
> git push origin main
Step 2: Generate a snapshot of content
Consider a snapshot as a directory of static content previously pulled from your content sources, which does not update itself.
> yarn gen:snapshot
Step 3: Configure environment for S3
> export MOSAIC_MODE="snapshot-s3"
> export MOSAIC_S3_BUCKET="<your S3 bucket id>"
> export MOSAIC_S3_REGION="<your S3 region>"
> export MOSAIC_S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID=""<your S3 access key>"
> export MOSAIC_S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY="<your S3 secret>"
> yarn mosaic upload -S ./snapshots/latest
Step 4: Setup AWS
Switch to the 
AWS Amplify
 console and deploy your app as a SSR application by following the 
AWS docs
Setup an S3 bucket as per the 
AWS S3 docs
Step 5: Configure your AWS app
Add the environment vars to the hosted app via your console
MOSAIC_MODE="snapshot-s3"
MOSAIC_S3_BUCKET="<your S3 bucket id>"
MOSAIC_S3_REGION="<your S3 region>"
MOSAIC_S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID=""<your S3 access key>"
MOSAIC_S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY="<your S3 secret access key>"
Add the following build settings
version: 1
frontend:
  phases:
    preBuild:
      commands:
        - yarn install
        - env | grep -e MOSAIC >> .env.production
    build:
      commands:
        - yarn run build
  artifacts:
    baseDirectory: .next
    files:
      - '**/*'
  cache:
    paths:
      - node_modules/**/*
Ensure the Node is set to 16
Step 6: Upload your snapshot
Upload your snapshot to S3 storage.
> yarn mosaic upload -S ./snapshots/latest

title: Admin
content:
There are several admin urls exposed by Mosaic that provide an insight into how the filesystem has been configured and a way to remotely manage sources.
Endpoints
| Endpoint                   | Method | Description                                  | Params                 |
| -------------------------- | ------ | -------------------------------------------- | ---------------------- |
         | GET    | Returns the JSON from the Mosaic config file | n/a                    |
   | GET    | Returns the entire mosaic filesystem as JSON | n/a                    |
   | GET    | Returns a collection of active sources       | n/a                    |
    | POST   | Adds the source                              | definition & isPreview |
    | PUT    | Stops the source with the provided name      | name                   |
 | PUT    | Restarts the source with the provided name   | name                   |

title: Git Repo Source
content:
The Git Repo Source is used to pull content from a remote git repository e.g. github.
Installation
Credentials and Access tokens
To successfully clone the git repo, the source definition must include credentials that have sufficient permissions to clone the repository.
We recommend storing a 
personal access token
 in an environment variable and using the environment variable in the source definition.
This keeps credentials out of code where they may be accidentally exposed to third parties.
Example
export MOSAIC_DOCS_CLONE_CREDENTIALS="<repo username>:<Personal Access Token (PAT) provided by your Repo OR password>",
Configuration
| Property            | Description                                                                      | Required |
| ------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------- |
| modulePath          | The path to the installed module (@jpmorganchase/mosaic-source-git-repo)         | Yes      |
| namespace           | The scope for this source.                                                       
| Yes      |
| disabled            | When true, content from this source is not used                                  | No       |
| options.credentials | Collection of URLS to make requests                                              | Yes      |
| options.prefixDir   | The root path used in the content URL                                            | Yes      |
| options.subfolder   | The name of the folder within the cloned repo containing the docs                | Yes      |
| options.repo        | The repo URL                                                                     | Yes      |
| options.branch      | The branch or tag to clone                                                       | Yes      |
| options.extensions  | Collection of file extensions that the source will look for inside the subfolder | Yes      |
| options.remote      | The name of the git remote to use. 
Defaults to origin.                           
| Yes      |
Example Git Repo Source Definition

 {
      modulePath: '@jpmorganchase/mosaic-source-git-repo',
      namespace: 'mosaic',
      options: {
        credentials: process.env.MOSAIC_DOCS_CLONE_CREDENTIALS,
        prefixDir: 'mosaic',
        subfolder: 'docs',
        repo: 'https://github.com/jpmorganchase/mosaic.git',
        branch: 'main',
        extensions: ['.mdx'],

title: Source Schedules
content:
A source schedule defines how often a source initiates a content pull and what to do when there is a failure.
A schedule can be specified for each source in the source definition, but should a source not provide a schedule it will inherit the "global" schedule.
Configuration
| Property          | Description                                                                            | Required | Default |
| ----------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------- | ------- |
| checkIntervalMins | The length of time in minutes before triggering a content refresh                      | Yes      | 30 mins |
| initialDelayMs    | Startup delay for the source.                                                          
| Yes      | 1000 ms |
| retryEnabled      | When true, failures will trigger another content pull                                  | No       | true    |
| retryDelayMins    | The interval between retries. 
This will rise exponentially on every failure.           
| No       | 5       |
| maxRetries        | Maximum number of retry attempts                                                       | No       | 100     |
| resetOnSuccess    | If true, when a source recovers and emits pages it's retry counter is returned to zero | No       | true    |
Global Schedule
The global schedule applies to all sources that do 
not
 provide their own schedule. 
It can be configured as a top-level property of the Mosaic config file.
 schedule: {
    checkIntervalMins: 60,
    initialDelayMs: 1000,
    retryDelayMins: 15,
    maxRetries: 20
Example
Given the config file below:
 schedule: {
    checkIntervalMins: 30,
    initialDelayMs: 1000,
    retryDelayMins: 5,
    maxRetries: 10
  },
  sources: [
    {
      modulePath: '@jpmorganchase/mosaic-source-git-repo',
      namespace: 'sourceA',
      options: {
        credentials: 'credentials',
        prefixDir: 'sourceA',
        subfolder: 'docs',
        repo: 'source-a-repo-url',
        branch: 'develop',
        extensions: ['.mdx'],
        remote: 'origin'
      }
    },
    {
      modulePath: '@jpmorganchase/mosaic-source-git-repo',
      namespace: 'sourceB',
      schedule:{
        checkIntervalMins: 60,
        initialDelayMs: 5000,
        retryDelayMins: 30,
        maxRetries: 50
      }
      options: {
        credentials: 'credentials',
        prefixDir: 'sourceB',
        subfolder: 'docs',
        repo: 'source-b-repo-url',
        branch: 'develop',
        extensions: ['.mdx'],
        remote: 'origin'
      }
    }
Source A will inherit the global schedule so it will:
Start after a 1 second delay
Pull content every 30 minutes
Retry a failed content pull after an initial 5 minute delay
Retry 10 times and if still unsuccessful, closing
Source B has its own schedule so it will:
Start after a 5 second delay
Pull content every 60 minutes
Retry a failed content pull after an initial 30 minute delay
Retry 50 times and if still unsuccessful, closing
Retry Strategy
The retry strategy that Mosaic employs is 
Exponential Backoff
This is a common strategy for networking applications that aims to prevent retries from causing more harm than good.
For example, given a source schedule that has a 1 minute retry delay and will retry a maximum of 3 times then the total time spent retrying is 7 minutes:
1 minute delay then 1st retry
2 minute delay then 2nd retry
4 minute delay then 3rd (and final) retry
Total delay: 1 + 2 + 4 = 7 minutes
As you can see, the delay between retries is growing exponentially giving the content source more time to recover after each retry.

title: $afterSource
content: The first lifecycle event to trigger after receiving pages from a source and runs in a child process.
The pages can safely be mutated and will be reflected in the final filesystem that gets generated.
pages - the collection of pages emitted by the source
helpers - an object with useful methods
options - the options specified for the plugin in the mosaic config file
The helpers provided with this lifecycle event are listed in the table below.
for serialising/deserialising pages when reading/writing to the filesystem                                         |
| config         | A mutable object for sharing data with other lifecycle phases of all plugins for this source (including in the main thread) in this plugin |
| pageExtensions | A collection of pageExtensions the source is using                                                                                         |
| ignorePages    | A collection of page globs that are to be ignored for this source                                                                          |
| namespace      | The namespace of the source running the plugin                                                                                             |
Example - Log out all page routes

title: afterUpdate
content: The third lifecycle event to trigger overall and the first to trigger inside the main Mosaic process.
Calls after the filesystem and symlinks have been reconstructed due to a change to the current source pages.
be cached when read at this stage, to allow for reading content and writing a new copy of it without the cached version taking effect.
This method is safe to use with lazy loading, as the filesystem should return the full page when read.
mutableFilesystem - Mutable filesystem instance with all of this source's pages inside (and symlinks re-applied)
helpers - an object with useful methods
options - the options specified for the plugin in the mosaic config file
The helpers provided with this lifecycle event are listed in the table below.
for serialising/deserialising pages when reading/writing to the filesystem                                                                  |

| globalConfig     | An immutable object for reading data from other lifecycle phases of all plugins.
| sharedFilesystem | Mutable filesystem instance independent of any sources.
Useful for global pages, like sitemaps                                                                      |

title: Lifecycle Events
content: The plugin lifecycle is triggered when a source emits content.
Each Mosaic source has its own worker thread and plugin lifecycle events that start with a
will execute inside the worker thread.
All other lifecycle events will execute in the main Mosaic process.
Plugin methods that trigger inside the main thread should be asynchronous and highly optimised to
avoid holding up the main thread.

will call this lifecycle hook since there is no

title: Sunsetting the UI Toolkit
content: Sunsetting the UI Toolkit at the end of Q2 2026
Effective end of Q2 2026, the UI Toolkit (UITK) will be sunset.
This enables the Salt Design System team to focus fully on a modern, flexible, and performant frontend solution for the firm.
Below you’ll find what’s changing, why we’re doing it, and how to migrate smoothly to the
UITK enters sunset at the end of Q2 2026.
After this date, the Salt team will no longer provide centralized support, bug fixes, or releases for UITK.

How do UI Toolkit and Salt Patterns compare?
A Salt pattern is a guide that helps a team build a design solution for their project.
It offers a set of composable components that serve as the building blocks of patterns.
These patterns outline the components and features that can help a user achieve the intended solution.
The main difference between Salt patterns and UITK (UI Toolkit) patterns is in their distribution and implementation.
UITK patterns are typically distributed as code packages that can be directly used in a project.
They provide pre-built components and functionality that can be easily integrated into an application.
On the other hand, Salt patterns are not necessarily distributed as code packages.
Instead, they serve as guidelines for building design solutions.
The Salt team may provide high-quality coded implementations of these patterns as examples, but the focus is on empowering teams to use the provided tools as they see fit.
This approach offers increased flexibility, allowing teams to adapt and customize the patterns to their specific needs.
In summary, Salt patterns provide a flexible framework for building design solutions, while UITK patterns offer pre-built components and functionality that can be directly used in a project.

Can I use Salt with other JPM Design Systems ?
The Salt team is actively discussing with other JPM design systems for compatibility.
We expect to have more details on this soon, so check with your own Design team for guidance.
When you should start using Salt depends on your specific needs and requirements for your projects.
Here are some factors to consider:
If you want to use Salt as-is, with minimal customization, you can start using it now.
Salt provides a range of features and functionalities that can be used out of the box.
If you plan to extensively customize the theme and functionality of Salt, it may be worth waiting until Q2 2024.
At that time, more details about the roadmap and other communication channels will be available, which may help inform your decision.
If you have existing projects that you are looking to update or upgrade, it is recommended to start thinking about migrating to Salt.
However, the decision to migrate should be made on a team-by-team basis, taking into account the specific requirements and timelines of each project.
Ultimately, the decision to start using Salt should be based on your specific needs and the level of customization you require.
It may be helpful to evaluate the features and capabilities of Salt, consider your project timelines, and consult with your team to make an informed decision.
What happens if I don’t migrate to Salt?
If you decide not to migrate to Salt in your project, there are long-term consequences to consider:
UITK development has transitioned to a maintenance state, which means that it will not receive regular updates and improvements.
This could result in performance and security issues in the long run, as the dependencies used by UITK may become outdated and vulnerable to security threats.
By not utilizing Salt, you may accumulate technical and design debt in your project.

Technical debt refers to the additional work that will need to be done in the future to fix or enhance the codebase, while design debt refers to the additional work required to align the project with current design standards and best practi
This could make it more challenging to maintain and enhance your project in the future.

If you have an existing project that relies on UITK and you choose not to migrate to Salt, you will not be able to adopt the value created by Salt and may incur an increased cost of maintaining a stagnating standard.
Considering these factors, it is advisable to start considering the migration to Salt, especially for new projects.
By using Salt from the beginning, you can avoid potential issues and ensure that your project remains up-to-date with the latest technologies and best practices.
Salt's Lab package is an incubator for alpha changes in the Salt software.
It is a separate package from the Core Salt package and is intended for experimental features and functionality that are still in the early stages of development.
The Lab package allows users to test and provide feedback on these new features before they are considered stable and included in the Core Salt package.
It is important to note that the Lab package is
recommended for use in production environments.
Since the features in the Lab package are still in development, they may not be fully tested or stable, and there is a higher likelihood of encountering bugs or compatibility issues.
Using the Lab package in production could create dependencies on features that may change or be removed in future releases, potentially causing disruptions or breaking changes to your infrastructure.
For production environments, it is recommended to rely on the Core Salt package.
The Core package consists of stable releases that follow semantic versioning (semver) and adhere to the Salt design standards.
These releases have undergone extensive testing and are considered reliable and suitable for production use.
In summary, while the Lab package provides early access to new features and functionality, it is best suited for testing and experimentation purposes.
For production environments, it is advisable to rely on the stable releases of the Core Salt package.
UITK is now in a maintain state.
Version 33 of UITK, released in December 2023, was the last major version.
While we plan to continue supporting UITK in a limited maintenance capacity, we anticipate ending support for it by the end of 2026.
The UITK will always be available for download, but we will start recommending the use of Salt instead.
Before finalizing a clear deprecation timeline for UITK, we will hold a consultation with stakeholders across the business.

The adapter pattern is a technique used to integrate third-party libraries into a React application.

title: Our strategy
content: What follows is an introduction to Salt from our Design Director, Ben Hopwood.
Salt is an open source, J.P.
Morgan design system, built from the ground up against internal requirements, using industry best practice against known accessibility and design standards.
As the next-generation version of the established internal J.P.
Morgan UI Toolkit design system, Salt builds upon the success of its predecessor, which has been utilized to create over 1,200 websites and applications.
Salt improves on UITK in four key areas:
Performant, smaller footprint and quicker loading times than UITK
Reduced dependence on third-party libraries like MUI—no longer locked into old versions or stale APIs
Simplified set of core components that can form more complex patterns
Open source—supports the firm’s initiatives to engage with communities and improve the quality of our code
A contribution model that encourages others to contribute—not just the Salt team
Holistic, systematic styling through CSS tokens shared across Salt, no need for third-party libraries or component-specific overrides
Compositional approach enables support of specific LOB use cases without breaking components
Patterns approach makes it easier to create complex designs with existing components
Morgan brand aligned styles and approved by the J.P.
Supports and facilitates the delivery of WCAG 2.1 (AA) accessible products and applications
Styled by a simplified, semantic palette through characteristics
Stronger, published design foundations that drive the system
is an Open Source product developed through a partnership between DXD and Digital Platform.
What can I do with Salt ?
Salt serves as an enabling foundation that allows you to align with design standards and accelerate your delivery.
Salt intentionally does not cover every use-case out-of-the-box, but it provides an easy way for you to fill those gaps according to your specific requirements.
The most cost-effective approach is to use Salt as it is, without deviations from the Salt standards.
Deviating from the Salt standards may introduce design and development costs that could be mitigated.

However due to the composability of Salt's foundations, as an adopter of Salt, you have the ability to independently initiate your Salt adoption by building your own patterns using Salt's foundational components.
This approach allows you to tailor Salt to your specific needs and create customized solutions that align with both your project requirements and known standards.

Why did you Open Source it ?
The majority of previous design systems at J.P Morgan has  built upon Open Source design systems.
Salt is product/business agnostic and contains no proprietary information.
By open sourcing Salt, we not only enable other J.P.
Morgan products to be open sourced but also establish an instant contribution model, fostering collaboration and innovation across the bank.
Why did you call it Salt ?
The design system's name, "Salt", draws inspiration from its rich historical significance as a valuable commodity.
In addition to its historical connotations, the name Salt also evokes the idea of seasoning, adding flavor and enhancing the overall experience.
Salt but it's important to remember that Salt is not an acronym.

title: New optimized swatch order for the Categorical color palette
content: The Salt Categorical palette has been re-ordered.
While the individual color values and names remain the same, the sequence in which they are applied to data visualizations or components that support categories has been updated.
Feedback from users indicated that the colors could achieve greater visual distinction if their order was adjusted.
It was also observed that the original sequence placed a hue of teal (aqua) within the first four swatches, which is in the same family as the theme’s accent color.
This created a visual correlation that could unintentionally imply meaning.
By design, all Categorical colors have similar contrast levels, as they all use the 500 series swatch from their respective color ramps.
To address this, we used a machine learning model to generate various sequences optimized for visual distinction.
This generally resulted in an order that alternated between warmer and cooler colors, depending on the starting point.
We settled on an order that places the first aqua-like color past the midway point, assuming most data visualizations will display fewer than ten colors at once.
This helps ensure that the Categorical colors are not mistaken for the accent color.
Since this is considered a breaking change for users already utilizing the Categorical palette, the update will be implemented at a later date.
In the meantime, users who wish to take advantage of the new optimized order can manually adjust their applications using the mapping provided below.

title: Salt Next Theme Color palette revamp
content: In the Salt Next Theme we completely overhauled the base color ramps used to drive the semantic styles for Salt components, correcting the challenges of the current, UI Toolkit-aligned Salt theme.
: We aligned our colors with the J.P.
Reduced Number of Swatches per Ramp
: We streamlined the number of swatches for better usability.
: We ensured the swatches in the ramp are more evenly spaced.
: We met the required contrast ratios.
: We created equivalent ramps for easy mode switching.
We started by aligning the Salt 500 colors with the closest 500 colors from the JPM MasterBrand palette, which includes shades of gray, blue, teal, green, orange, red, and purple.
Although we preferred to use these colors directly, they did not meet the minimum contrast ratio requirement of 4.5:1 with black or white text.
This issue was also present in the current Salt palette.
Reduced Number of Swatches per Ramp
The current Salt palette had asymmetrical ramps, offering more color options below 500 than above, making it impossible to center the 500 swatch.
Additionally, the palette did not provide an equal number of colors for each ramp.
For example, the gray ramp had 18 swatches, while others had only 14, except for orange, which had 15.
Except for gray and orange, we maintained the hue of the MasterBrand 500 colors and adjusted the brightness and saturation to meet the minimum contrast ratio requirement.
Once we had our 500 swatches for each color, we moved on to the next issue.
We determined that there were too many options and insufficient visual differences between adjacent colors.
After a detailed audit, we found many colors were unused or used inconsistently, complicating systematic mode switching.
We concluded that nine swatches per ramp were optimal.
This allowed us to center 500 in the middle, with four colors below (100, 200, 300, 400) and four above (600, 700, 800, 900).
This also aligned with the J.P.
With our new 500 swatches, we used the J.P.

For the 900 colors, we used the MasterBrand 800 swatches as the starting point, keeping the hues as they were, setting the saturation to 100 (except for gray), and adjusting the brightness to achieve the desired results and contrast minimum
With our 100, 500, and 900 swatches established, we used the Chroma Tool to generate the remaining swatches (200, 300, 400, 600, and 700 series).
This tool ensures equally spaced values between colors, corrects lightness, and applies bezier interpolation.
We manually increased the saturation for the 200, 300, and 400 series to remove dullness.
Once the entire palette (100-900 for all colors) was created, we tested various color combinations in situ to see the results when applied to our components and sample UIs.
This process ensured the required contrast ratios were met for both decorative and informative scenarios.
If issues arose, we made fine adjustments and re-ran the ramps until achieving the desired visual results and required contrast ratios.
For example, colored text in secondary banners:
The final step was to invert the ramps, creating equivalents between light and dark modes for simple and consistent swapping.
This means a 100 color in one mode always equals a 900 color of the same ramp in the other, allowing for designing in one mode and getting the other for free.
The Final Salt Next Color Palette
Upon completion, the final color palette shown below was implemented into the Salt Next theme.

title: Introducing Business Library Managers
content: Business Library Managers (BLMs… catchy) are a new communication channel initiative to further increase transparency between delivery teams and the Salt design system and to facilitate knowledge sharing across LOBs.
Business Library Managers are identified individuals who oversee or influence the use of Salt’s components and tokens within a
These individuals represent a snapshot of
, and consumers of the design system, and form a first point of contact between the Salt team and LOB Business Libraries and their delivery teams.
Image 1: The Business Library Managers model.
The initiative provides BLMs with advance update of systematic, operational and strategical change that may impact application delivery.
Functional change which improves on a component.
Token updates which result in visual change.
Technical releases which impact design system consumption.
Support models which define engagement with the system.
In exchange, BLMs have an opportunity to:
Provide constructive feedback and critique relevant to their domain.
Influence the backlog through delivery schedules and requirements.
Manage how updates are communicated/ adopted within their teams.
How do BLMs engage with Salt?

BLMs are invited to a recurring forum with Salt leadership to provide consolidated business feedback to Salt Design System and to receive advance updates which they can distribute amongst their delivery teams.

This recurring forum provides your BLM with an opportunity to influence future strategy, backlog priority and DXD org wide comms, in addition to reviewing x-LOB Salt initiatives and identifying opportunities for collaboration.
BLMs are a new concept and the roles, responsibilities and identified library managers may change or evolve as the initiative becomes more established.
A list of our Designer and Engineering BLMs is
Business Library Managers reflect Salt’s ongoing commitment to provide delivery teams with visibility and support.
Your BLM is a first point of contact to accelerate feedback to the Salt team and to keep you up to date with the latest goings-on.
Please make your BLM aware of anything you think they should raise at a future Business Library Manager forum which would be beneficial across LOBs and improve the system.

title: Change is coming... new Figma libraries are on their way!
content: We are excited to announce an evolution in our Figma libraries.
We are introducing new variable-based libraries that seamlessly provide the two Salt themes out of the box, eliminating the need to set 'style options'.
The two themes of the new component library

The new library structure will give designers a single, consolidated variables-based theme library that is fully aligned with Salt code and continues to build on Salt's alignment with the JPMorgan brand.
This update reduces governance responsibilities for lead designers and enhances consistency across projects.
Additionally, the Salt theme based on legacy UITK will now be integrated within the same component library as the Salt next theme.

This consolidation allows us to reduce our Figma libraries from 13 to 6, vastly reducing the number of libraries designers have to reference, further promoting consistency and enabling the design system team to operate more efficiently.
Fewer libraries to reference and manage
The new libraries are being created to allow for the following existing libraries to be retired:
| Figma libraries to be retired | New Salt DS libraries |
| Salt (Next) Component and Patterns library | Salt DS Components and Patterns |
| Salt (Next) Styles library | Salt DS Themes |
| Salt Color library | Salt DS Legacy (UITK) Colors |
| Salt (Next) Color library | Salt DS JPM Brand Colors |
| Salt JPMC Logos | Salt DS Logos |
In addition to reducing the number of libraries, we are also reducing the variable options available to designers.
Currently, the Salt (Next) Library has 128 possible combinations a designer can choose from.
We're reducing the variable collections to three: Theme, Mode, and Density.
This will reduce the possible combinations to just 16.
We're achieving this by combining the 'styling options' in the Salt Next theme to two themes that are ready to use out-the-box: Legacy (UITK) and JPM Brand.
The same themes are achieved in code using the SaltProvider and SaltProviderNext components.
Simplified theme selection in the new Figma component library
Why are we making this change?
This update will streamline design processes for Salt design consumers and the Salt Design Team.
Ease of migration and library set up
: The new components support both UITK (Legacy) and JPM Brand themes.
There is no longer a need to install multiple libraries.
Simply change swap between the two themes and see components instantly update.
If you’re using the UITK (Legacy) theme to migrate a UITK application, this theme capability will enable you to instantly swap your designs to the JPM brand theme once your migration is complete.
Alignment to JPM brand and simplified theme selection
: No longer a need to set multiple styling options to define the brand theme–it comes configured out-the-box.
: With clearly defined themes out-the-box, design leads only need to direct teams to a specific theme and ensure development partners are informed of the appropriate theme to reference.
: Fewer libraries for the Salt design team to manage and update means we can ensure the quality of the libraries and spend more time on features for app delivery teams.
: With fewer libraries to manage, the component and pattern creation times will be reduced.
Documentation and QA testing will also be more efficient as themes, modes and densities can be switched easily within the same library.
We understand that introducing new libraries shortly after the last release may seem abrupt.
However, feedback from design leads and the current limitations of Figma left us with limited options.
Before proceeding, we carefully considered several alternatives:
Work on the live Figma libraries by updating the Salt (Next) libraries
: Designers have already begun migrating, and feedback has been positive.
There would be no need to promote new libraries.
: Frequent updates would be required for testing and iteration, potentially disrupting existing designs without warning.
Errors could necessitate rollbacks, causing further disruption.
Changes might also break existing business libraries built on top of Salt Figma libraries.
Duplicate components by copying each component or pattern and adding a 'theme' version to the library
: No need to duplicate entire libraries, resulting in minimal disruption.
Multiple style libraries with the same names could cause confusion.
Designers might inadvertently mix components, requiring more guidance.
Migration pathways would be challenging, and libraries would become much 'heavier'.
Update components individually by switching each to the new style library in turn
: Allows for a migration roadmap to the new libraries, resulting in less immediate disruption.
: Multiple libraries and options would still be displayed when setting variable modes.
The full library release would take much longer, and business libraries would still need updates, spreading inconvenience over a longer period.
What is the impact of this change?
It's important to state, with this update
the design of the components and patterns are not changing
Reducing the number of Figma libraries
Simplifying visual design specs by removing style options in Figma and replacing with a theme choice
Continuing Salt's commitment to align with the brand
Helping teams migrate from UITK to Salt
Designers using any Light, Dark or Next Salt libraries directly
Business Libraries providing domain specific patterns built on Salt Figma components
When can you expect this change?
New libraries ready, stable and published at
Existing libraries marked as retired immediately following release.
Existing libraries unpublished end of day
We will provide migration guidance to help you through this change.
We recommend planning your migration before existing libraries are unpublished.
We'll be on hand to help.
Salt will release a consolidated set of libraries in Figma by EOY.
The new libraries will initially support two themes.
The themes will focus on UITK migration and JPM Brand alignment.
13 Salt libraries will be reduced to 6.
All previous libraries to be retired immediately, and unpublished on Monday January 6th.

title: Salt Figma Design Assets Naming Update—Introducing Template
content: To improve clarity and usability across the Salt Design System, we’ve updated the naming of our pattern assets in Salt DS Components and Patterns Figma library—formerly called
This change is part of a broader effort to align design system language with both how designers use these assets in Figma and how we anticipate Figma’s features evolving.
You can see the research summary in
Our previous terminology—particularly “Stickers”—caused confusion among consumers.
During our recent research, we learned that “Sticker” was interpreted in various ways.
Consumers weren’t always sure what could be detached, or how to better configure the assets, with some uncertainty about the difference between patterns and components in both design and code.
We also discussed these challenges with the Figma team.

Their guidance reaffirmed that Template is a more appropriate term for assets meant to be reused, detached, and configured, which aligns with planned future Figma updates (e.g., potential template-specific features).
| Salt DS Figma artifact | Definition | Figma Library | Figma library example |
| Component | Salt components distributed as Figma components.
| Salt DS Components & Patterns Library  | Avatar, Banner, Button |
| Template | Salt components AND patterns distributed as Figma components.
to customize the composition (e.g., add or remove elements) | Salt DS Components & Patterns Library | Checkbox group template, Data Grid template |
| Sticker | Patterns built by Salt (or contributions) available as example frames.
| Salt DS Pattern Stickersheets | Forms, International Address Form |                          |
We will be creating a dedicated Salt DS Pattern Stickersheets file that consolidates reusable example designs (like forms, international address forms).
This will make it easier for teams to find common patterns and contribute their own, with the goal of keeping things intuitive, practical and easy to use.

title: Enhancing Salt icon discoverability with intuitive search
content: We're excited to share an upgrade to Salt's icon set - you can now search for icons on the Salt website and in Figma using synonyms as well as browse icons by category in Figma.
With the addition of icon synonyms and categories it'll be far easier to find the icon you're looking for.
Our community has shared feedback about the challenges in searching for icons.
Users often struggle to find the right icon without knowing its exact name, leading to frustration when searches don't yield desired results.
This highlights a gap in our content, making navigation difficult and reducing user confidence.
We're committed to improving this experience for everyone.
We’re introducing lightweight categories to every icon component in Figma.
These categories serve as high-level groupings, such as “People” and “Places,” to streamline your search experience.
Our ‘Salt DS Assets’ Figma library is now organized into 15 distinct categories which you can easily toggle off if you prefer to browse the full set.
We’ve ensured that the category names are aligned for cohesion with other design system icon categories at the firm such as
While each icon could arguably belong in multiple categories, Figma restricts assets to be associated with one group.
As these categories are currently only in Figma, we welcome constructive feedback if you feel certain icons would be better placed in different categories or if the category names could be improved.
To further enhance your experience, we've added synonyms to each icon to boost findability.
This will ensure you can quickly and efficiently find the icons you need, regardless of the variations in naming.
The synonyms included for each icon are:
Functional: The core action or use-case the icon supports.
Visual: The icon’s appearance or shape – what it visually represents.
Contextual: The context the icon is used in, e.g. navigation.
Related terms: Spelling variations based on localization, e.g. cookie, biscuit, or check, cheque.
Additionally, we’ve matched our icons against those in JPM Styleguide and
Shared synonyms were harmonized according to where concepts overlap such as “share,” “search” and “settings.”
Products transitioning between different design systems within the firm may face difficulties in maintaining consistency and this aims to improve multi-system search coverage.

By adding functional, visual and contextual related terms into each icon description in Figma, you can now simply type a descriptive term into the search bar in Figma's asset panel, and all relevant icons will be displayed.
These synonyms have also been added to the icon search available in the
on the Salt Design System website.
No matter what you’re building, we’ve made it easier to discover what’s already in the system – and spend more time creating, not hunting.
We’re committed to continuously improving the Salt icon library to better serve our design community.

title: Introducing the Cursor foundation
content: The Salt Design System is committed to continuous improvement, and we're pleased to announce the addition of a new foundation: Cursor.
This update addresses previous challenges with cursor behavior specification, aiming to streamline and enhance the design and development experience.
Previously, cursor behaviors were defined within individual
, leading to duplication, misunderstanding, and misuse.
Visibility was a concern, as designers and developers often struggled to identify the appropriate cursor tokens for various situations.
The Cursor Foundation consolidates all cursor behaviors within Salt, providing a centralized and clear definition of cursor interactions.
By defining 10 cursor behaviors as a foundation, we've eliminated over twice as many tokens, simplifying the design system and enhancing usability.
The Cursor Foundation governs how the cursor appears when positioned over or interacting with components.
This behavior is relevant for web browsers and operating systems that display cursors in the user interface.
| not-allowed | Disabled or selected disabled states |
| ew-resized | Hover and active states of a draggable component restricted to horizontal movement |
| ns-resized | Hover and active states of a draggable component restricted to vertical movement |
| grab | Hover state of a draggable object |
| grabbing | Active state of a draggable object |
| pointer | The default cursor state when hovering over an interactable component |
| progress | Indicates that the system is busy processing a task and the user should wait for it to complete |
| text | Indicates where text can be inserted, selected or edited |
This update will streamline cursor behavior across the Salt Design System, reducing complexity and enhancing clarity.
The centralized cursor tokens will ensure consistent interactions and improve the overall user experience.

content: The Salt Design System continues to thrive, evolving to meet the growing interest and diverse needs of our users.
As we expand, we're excited to introduce updates to our foundational Size and Spacing tokens, enhancing flexibility and consistency across components, patterns, and theme implementations.
Historically, our size and spacing tokens have been guided by Salt's '

Density influences the amount of information displayed on the screen.
However, as Salt has matured, the demand for tokens with fixed values across all densities has emerged.

Fixed values are also crucial for component spacing.
In developing components such as numerical input, fixed-spacing ensures precise pixel values for gaps between parts, enhancing design consistency.

title: Introduction to brown
content: Morgan Brown is our core color, derived from our heritage brand.
It is a distinctive and recognizable color that sets us apart in the predominantly blue landscape of the financial services industry.
Morgan Brown is utilized thoughtfully and selectively, such as in our logo, and is never the dominant color in our materials and communications.
To support the use of brown within the Salt Design System, we have introduced a brown foundational ramp as part of a beta release.
As with all our foundational ramps, we strive to align them as closely as possible with the J.P.
Morgan Flagship Brand color palette, making adjustments only as needed to meet ADA contrast requirements.
In the case of brown, the first swatch in the JPM Brand palette (brown-50) also functions as the tertiary background color (limestone).

Within the Salt Design System, background swatches are independent from the foundational ramps, enabling their use for 'states' and 'fills' in components and ensuring they remain visually distinct when overlaid on background colors.
As a result, Salt has introduced a new brown-100, situated between limestone and brown-200.
This adjustment shifts the swatch numbering by one space, leading to JPM Brand’s brown-100 corresponding to Salt’s brown-200.
Below is a list that outlines the mapping between the two ramps:
| JPM Brand brown | Hex value | Salt token | Hex value |
The brown values featured in the beta release are displayed below.
Please note that this does not include JPM-brown and limestone, as these are managed separately from the foundational ramp, as previously discussed.
In the Salt Design System, brown is categorized as a sentiment and labeled as 'brand'.
This classification allows it to coexist with 'accent', which uses teal, enabling both colors to be used simultaneously in the same UI design.
Below is the complete list of Salt sentiments and their corresponding colors:
The Salt Legacy Theme serves as a transitional theme to facilitate the migration from UITK to the Salt JPM Brand Theme.
As a result, both accent and brand sentiments in Legacy are aligned to blue to maintain compatibility.
To incorporate brown and teal, you will need to use the JPM Brand Theme.
Brown (brand) is intended as a complementary color to teal (accent) and will be available only in select components to ensure it doesn't become dominant.
Except for buttons and toggle buttons, it will primarily be used for decorative purposes.
However, it should be applied thoughtfully to add warmth or highlight important elements or words throughout the application.

Initially, there is no impact on users of the design system.
Brown has been released as a beta in code and in the Salt DS JPM Brand Colors Figma library, but it is not yet available in any components.

title: Updates to Button's interaction states now live
content: We’re excited to announce a significant update to Salt Design System’s Button components, including Button, Segmented Button Group, Pill, and Toggle Button.
These changes are designed to improve clarity, accessibility, and ease of use across your applications.
The updates are now available in both code and Figma—no action is required on your part to benefit from these enhancements.
Button components are now optimized for light and dark modes
– Previously, Salt’s Button styles were ‘mode-agnostic’, supporting mixed mode usage.
With this update, hover and active states are tailored to the mode they’re used in, while default states remain unchanged to support mixed mode applications.
– Button types are now easier to recognize and distinguish, with improved interaction feedback and increased text contrast for better accessibility.
These improvements apply to Button, Segmented Button Group, Pill, and Toggle Button.
Image 1: Updated design for Hover and Active button states
– Instead of changing each attribute (foreground, background, border) to a ‘disabled’ token, the entire Button now shifts to 40% opacity when disabled.
– This change streamlines code and reduces the total number of design tokens by 65, representing a ~10% reduction in color tokens within Salt.
– Disabled tokens are now deprecated in code.
In Figma, disabled variables are prefixed with ‘DEPRECATED’ and will remain for 3 sprints (6 weeks) before removal.
This will not affect your design files, but references to these variables will no longer be connected to the theme library after this period.
Image 2: Reconciled Disabled styling approach for Button
– Toggle Button now includes a visually distinct ‘selected’ state, making it easier to differentiate from the solid Button appearance.
– Toggle Button now features an ‘active’ state that appears when pressed, improving user feedback.
Image 3: Updated design for Hover, Active & Selected toggle button states
What do you need to do?
No action required for code or Figma updates
– Simply update to the latest version of Salt DS Theme library to access the new features.
For Figma users referencing disabled variables
– After updating, you’ll see these variables prefixed with ‘DEPRECATED’.
They will be removed after 6 weeks.
We plan to extend these efficiency improvements to other areas of Salt Design System, further reducing complexity and streamlining your workflow.
Thank you for your continued feedback and support.
If you have any questions or need guidance, please reach out to the Salt Design System team.

title: Changes to Salt themes with Figma Extended Collections
content: Figma is introducing Extended Collections to JPMorganChase this month.
The new features will facilitate managing multi-brand design systems.
Extended Collections enable designers within a company to add their own styles to a foundational design system and then publish and reuse them.
Importantly, these extensions stay in sync with the parent design system, inheriting updates such as new variables or color changes, while preserving any custom overrides.
JPMorganChase employees will soon have access to Extended Collections.
For the Salt DS team, this is a very positive step.
We’ll be able to extend our existing theme support, building on work we’ve already trialed with our ‘Lab’ theme, which is currently being used to test new support for the
We’ve been working closely with Figma and our engineering partners across multiple LOBs to define a solution that works for both design and development.
While anyone will be able to extend a library collection, we recommend doing so thoughtfully, with consideration for how extended styles are managed across environments.
Extended Collections bring several benefits, including easier theme management and better alignment between design and code.
However, we understand that supporting the update will require changes to our libraries.
Rest assured, we’re committed to minimizing any impact on your workflow.
We’ll respond quickly to any issues and work closely with our partners at Figma to put together clear guidance.
This will enable us to move swiftly once Extended Collections functionality is made available.
: Please do not extend any Salt collections until we confirm the libraries are compatible.
Extending a theme library collection prematurely is likely to result in breakages when we make necessary changes to Salt.
We’ve already started making changes behind the scenes to Salt themes in preparation for the release.
Foundational variables have been separated into a new ‘Salt DS Shared Foundations’ library, aligning our theme structure in design more closely with code.
We’re also cleaning up and reducing the number of tokens ('Figma variables') needed to style Salt, making theme extension and application more intuitive.
Our documentation on Salt themes and tokens is being overhauled, with the first phase releasing soon.
In Figma, we’ve added usage guidance for every color variable in the theme, to help designers understand each style’s intended use.
We’ll announce all changes to the theme library in our public Teams channel and provide plenty of notice there and in our Salt newsletter.

title: Introducing Salt Code Connect - Bridging Figma Design and Code
content: Are you a designer or developer who still finds handoff a bit painful?
Salt is working with the AI for Design team to use Figma Code Connect to make Salt components easier to align, understand, and implement.

By leveraging AI to efficiently generate internal-ready code from Salt Figma components, we’re streamlining designer–developer collaboration and enabling a faster, more consistent delivery process across the firm.
Salt Code Connect links Salt Figma components directly to their internal code implementations.
Built in partnership with the AI for Design team, using Figma Code Connect and (future) MCP-based dev tooling.
Goal: reduce ambiguity in handoff and make it easier to build with Salt correctly, the first time.
Phase 1 (in progress): establish trusted Code Connect mappings and a sustainable maintenance model.
Phase 2 (upcoming): enable MCP-based workflows where Copilot can generate internal code directly from Figma designs.
We’re looking for teams to pilot and to join our research study.
Interested in piloting for initial testing + research of Salt Code Connect?
For project info & Salt Figma library questions, reach out to Yun-Jung Yeh (yun-jung.yeh@jpmorgan.com) & Reva Shakti (reva.shakti@jpmorgan.com).
This initiative has two main phases:
We're implementing Figma Code Connect for Salt components and putting a sustainable governance and maintenance plan in place.
The goal is to ensure that when a designer or developer looks at a Salt component in Figma, they can trust that the linked code and documentation are accurate and up to date.
Enabling AI-powered code generation from Figma:

Once MCP access is available within the firm, we'll provide guidance for using an MCP-based dev tool (via Copilot agents) that can generate internal code directly from Figma files that use Salt components.
This is where we move from "better handoff" to "assisted implementation".
Spending extra time creating detailed final specs for foundational pages and specific edge cases.
Not always knowing how much detail engineers actually need, or how closely the design maps to existing code.
Answering repeated questions like “Is this the standard Salt version?”
or “Does this variant exist in code?”
Interpreting design specs and trying to guess the intended component, props, and variants.
Hunting through repos or asking around to find the “right” implementation.
Risk of choosing a similar-looking but incorrect component, which creates subtle inconsistencies over time.
A strong Salt Figma library used across many teams.
A robust Salt codebase powering production experiences.
a seamless link between the two.
Salt uses Figma Code Connect plus AI support to:
Turn the design system into one connected source of truth from design to implementation.
Reduce back-and-forth and manual detective work.
Help teams ship consistent, Salt-aligned experiences faster and with more confidence the first time.
is a feature that links Figma components directly to the code behind them.
It bridges codebase and Figma’s Dev Mode, connecting design components to their real code counterparts for better consistency and collaboration.

Engineers can jump from the design to the correct implementation and documentation, without guesswork.

title: Introducing the next-generation of Salt Patterns
content: We’re excited to announce the launch of the next-generation of
: a new layer of the Salt Design System focused on reusable, enterprise-ready UI layouts that solve typical UI use cases in CIB applications.
Unified CIB focus on delivering patterns
Patterns compress time to market by turning common UX problems into ready-made, proven building blocks, so teams can spend their effort on differentiation rather than reinvention.
Unified support for the upcoming J.P.
What the Salt Patterns workstream will provide
Salt Patterns are ready-to-use compound components for CIB applications, built on the Salt Design System.
They give teams a fast, consistent way to build common page structures—without reinventing layout, responsiveness, or accessibility each time.
Image 1 - Combining patterns to accelerate application build and delivery
Each pattern is built from Salt foundations, tokens, components, accessibility standards, and engineering guidance—helping teams deliver consistent, scalable, and accessible experiences faster.
We've just released the Browse Panel (see below), and are currently working on Chat UI and Page Header.
To make sure we’re focusing on the right patterns and prioritizing what you need, you can now make requests using the firm’s go/featurerequest tool at
A new flexible approach to patterns
provide application teams with flexible guidelines, which can be implemented as described or extended/amended for specific user needs.
While flexible, they don’t provide a repeatable, reusable UI solution that can be used out-of-the-box in application builds.
Patterns are delivered in a new package and consist of layouts of semantic slots, with rules designed to hold specific components.
Patterns are built so that AI models can understand these rules and generate consistent patterns for individual user needs across the business.
Salt will provide variations for each pattern that cover the most common use cases, but we know we can’t cater for every nuance.
In these cases, teams can add their own slots to pattern layouts and contribute them back to Salt Patterns for others to benefit from.
What each pattern will consist of
Salt Patterns provide governed, reusable building blocks that teams adopt instead of building from scratch.
Title, Actions, Navigation) so teams know exactly what goes where
— automatic adaptation from desktop to mobile with no additional work
— ESLint rules catch usage errors in the IDE before code reaches production
— describe a pattern in a spec file and AI agents generate the component code, layouts, ESLint rules, Storybook stories, and documentation automatically
— patterns follow Salt accessibility standards out of the box
— each pattern is published to the Salt DS Figma library with accompanying guides and examples
Introducing the first pattern: Browse Panel
is a pattern for browsing nested content alongside a primary work surface.

It composes a header layout (defined for browsing and exploring content) with a Salt Side Panel to give users a consistent way to drill into sections, track where they are in the hierarchy, and move between peer views — without leaving the
Image 2 - Browse Panel is the first next generation pattern for Salt Patterns

As a pattern, it governs how location, navigation, and contextual actions are arranged in the side surface: the page stays in focus, while the Browse Panel provides the standard shape, slots, and behaviour for the accompanying content.

Browse Panel has been designed, developed, and tested with partners from Payments and Global Banking businesses, and also used to validate the new technical approach used to implement these new Salt Patterns.
Complementing this work, we are also merging
Pepper Patterns into the Salt Design System
By bringing these expertise together, Salt Patterns will accelerate the creation of business patterns for CIB.
This will reduce duplication, strengthen consistency, and provide teams with a clearer path to adopt and extend enterprise patterns across applications.

title: What is Salt's Business Pattern
content: Salt's Business Pattern Index, available at
, is a platform to showcase prior art created with Salt.
Its main objective is to promote visibility and reusability of UI components, patterns, and resources across different products and organizations.
Currently, Salt's Business Pattern Index offers several features:
Deep linking to individual elements within a Figma spec:
This allows users to directly access specific components or sections within a Figma design.
Deep linking to individual Storybook Stories:
Users can navigate directly to specific stories within a Storybook instance, making it easier to find and reference specific UI components.
Linking to a ReadMe.md inside BitBucket:
Salt's Business Pattern Index provides links to
files within BitBucket repositories, allowing users to discover Salt related resources.
Linking to a documentation structure within BitBucket:
Users can also create their own documentation pages within the Salt site by configuring their own BitBucket documentation repositories, making it easier to find relevant information.
Filtering contents by source type, owner, and specific tags:
Salt's Business Pattern Index allows users to filter and search for specific UI components, patterns, or resources based on their source, ownership, or assigned tags.
Salt's Business Pattern Index is a
that regularly pulls content from registered sources during runtime to ensure it always displays the latest state.
The currently supported sources are Storybook, Figma, and BitBucket.
To add content to the index, contributors need to perform a one-time configuration of the data source.
This allows Salt's Business Pattern Index to automatically pull future changes from the registered source without requiring any additional effort from the contributor.
The setup process varies based on the source type:
Contributors need to register their Figma page group so that Salt's Business Pattern Index can retrieve changes from it.
Contributors need to register their Storybook instance and configure their Storybook deployment via ACM (Application Configuration Management) to enable runtime access to the Stories.
Contributors need to register their BitBucket ReadMe.md file and their BitBucket documentation repository.
This allows Salt's Business Pattern Index to access the repositories and pull changes from them.

title: Contribute an icon
content: Missing an icon in the Salt Design System?
You can propose your own icon designs by following our simple guidelines.
to see if your idea already exists.
If it's missing, you can create and contribute a new icon.
Ensure new icons are unique and universally applicable.
Icons specific to an app or use-case should be added to your own code repository, not the Salt assets.
These icons should follow this guide, but will need to be added to your own repository as an SVG.
Salt typically releases icons in batches relating to a particular subject, function, or behavior rather than icon-by-icon.
This should not be considered a blocker as individual icons can be created and stored in a repository and then replaced if and when its added to Salt assets.
If you think your icon proposal should be included in the Salt icon library, please follow these steps:
Ensure no similar or conflicting icons already exist.
Ensure the icon is named consistently with the icon library and is universally applicable.
Suggest icon name synonyms, this will be added as search terms to help others discover and use your icons.
Provide a use case; consider what the intended use for the icon is and why no existing icons provide by Salt are appropriate.
Ensure the icon follows existing designs and aligns to commonly accepted standards if relevant e.g. a pencil to represent editing an object.
Provide a solid variant, if applicable.
Consider other possible variants to help provide a cohesive set of icons - for instance, if submitting an 'add filter' icon, it may also be helpful to provide a 'remove filter' icon.
Salt icons are designed to be easily recognizable at a small size of 12px, supporting data-dense app experiences and use cases.
This size is the standard for both high and medium densities and represents the minimum size used throughout the design system.
To begin designing an icon, use a 12x12 grid as your canvas.
Ensure that all elements fit within this 12x12 bounding box to maintain consistency and clarity across the design system, especially in data-dense environments.
Salt icons should be based on standard shapes like squares, circles, and rectangles, each with consistent sizes.
With the minimum icon size of 12x12 pixels, aim to utilize the entire bounding box area.
Salt icons typically do not include padding, so ensure your design fills the space effectively for optimal visibility and consistency.
To support the creation of consistent icons, use a key-line grid.
This template standardizes the size, shape, position, and alignment of icons, ensuring a cohesive appearance across the design system.
To maximize clarity, try to position icon elements on whole pixels whenever possible.
Set the X and Y coordinates as whole numbers, avoiding decimal places.
Additionally, align vector nodes to whole pixels to maintain sharpness.
This should help to keep your icon crisp and precise.
Given that the base display size of an icon is 12 pixels, focus on using minimal shapes and strokes to ensure clarity and recognizability.
When depicting a physical object, represent it as a flat icon without any sense of depth.
This approach maintains simplicity and ensures that icons remain clear and effective at small sizes.
When designing a new icon, consider the following elements to ensure consistency:
: The lines that form the design of the icon.
: The negative spaces that suggest a line.
: The negative space within the icon.
: The end caps of lines that do not connect to another element in the icon.
: Points where the angle of a line changes.
: The radius of the outside edge of a corner.
: The radius of the inside edge of a corner.
Salt icons feature two corner types: sharp and curved, each serving a specific role in maintaining the design system's visual style.
For icons representing documents or similar physical objects, a corner can be folded over.
This design element visually links document types across the icons.
The primary corner style is sharp, predominantly used to convey the clean, crisp, and precise aesthetic of the Salt Design System.
Curves are sometimes needed to differentiate an icon or accurately represent a physical object.
When applying a corner radius, ensure that interior and exterior corners are parallel curves.
Depending on the icon, set the corner radius to either 1 or 2 pixels, based on a 12x12 pixel bounding box.
To ensure uniformity and clarity, use a stroke width of 1px when designing a 12x12 pixel icon.
In some cases, a thicker stroke may be necessary to align centrally with a shape or to emphasize a part of the icon.
Conversely, thinner strokes might be needed, such as for clock hands.
Use both thicker and thinner strokes judiciously to maintain the overall balance and consistency of the icon set.
Counter strokes should adhere to the same guidelines as standard strokes to ensure consistency in line weight and visual balance across the icon set.
This uniformity helps maintain a cohesive and harmonious design system.
When strokes need to be angled, set them at 45 degrees.
This standard angle helps maintain consistency across the icon set.
: Stroke terminals should always be flat, not rounded, to maintain a clean and precise appearance.
: The angle of stroke terminals should be set to 90 degrees.
The only exception is when a stroke is intersected by a counter stroke, where adjustments may be necessary to maintain visual coherence.
Most icons in the Salt Design System are available in two variants: outline and solid.
When designing a Salt icon, begin with the outline version, as it serves as the foundational style for most scenarios.
If feasible, create a solid variant to offer greater choice and flexibility.
Solid icons are useful for indicating toggle controls or providing greater prominence, such as highlighting a status like an error state.
However, not all icons can have both variants; for example, directional icons typically only have an outline option.
It’s important that any outlines have been turned into shapes (to help scale the icons).
Include a grouped and flattened version of the icon, as this simplifies the integration process.
In certain cases, it may be necessary to include alphanumeric characters within an icon, such as indicating a file type like CSV.
Use these characters sparingly and only when absolutely necessary.
When incorporating typographic elements, use the Open Sans font with a semiBold weight and a font size of 7 pixels, based on the minimum icon size of 12x12 pixels.
Limit the number of characters to no more than three within an icon to ensure readability.
Set letter spacing to 0, but in some instances, you may need to adjust it to a negative value to fit all characters comfortably within the icon's design.
When contributing an icon to Salt, it's essential to name it thoughtfully to ensure universal applicability.
Please avoid specific references to JPM and instead focus on the icon’s broader context.
Align your naming with standards from other icon sets within the firm or universally, ensuring consistency and familiarity.
Since the introduction of synonyms to the icon library set, we encourage you to add suggested synonyms for your icon to enhance findability.
For guidance on this, please refer to
Enhancing Salt icon discoverability with intuitive search
Clearly defining the icon's name, its solid variant (if applicable), and relevant synonyms will help speed up the contribution process.
Before submitting your icon proposal, it's highly recommended to run the Salt Icon Contribution Checker Figma Plugin, located on the internal site under
This tool ensures that your icon can be contributed easily and accurately by verifying the following conditions:
Icon size and aspect ratio: The icon must be set to 12 x 12 pixels, with the aspect ratio locked to maintain consistent dimensions.
Color Consistency: The icon should use the correct color variable and must not contain any unauthorized colors.
Single Child Layer: Ensure that the icon consists of only one child layer.
Flattened for Export: The icon should be flattened and ready for export.
Vector Format: The child layer must be in vector format.
Correct Naming: The child layer should be named appropriately to facilitate icon swapping.
Scalability: The child layer must be scalable without losing quality.
: The plugin also makes sure that vertices aren’t on half values.
SVG vertices with long decimal places can cause aliasing issues which affects exported SVG.
Although shown as equal to all other checks within the plugin this condition is purely advisory and can be ignored if the ‘fix’ fundamentally changes the structure of the icon.
By following these guidelines, you can contribute high-quality icons to the Salt Design System that are consistent, clear, and visually harmonious.

This ensures we can swiftly respond to your request.
Share that with our team by sending a link to your Figma file and a brief description to the

, Salt provides a template for business patterns that can be used to standardize the way business library patterns are consumed across CIB app delivery teams, and which can be used to publish patterns to Salt’s Business Pattern Index (BPI).
Image 1: Use Salt’s business pattern template to document and share you patterns in your business
To start using the template, you should:
Enable the Salt DS Spec Utilities library in Figma to gain access to the template and spec components.

Before getting started with the Business Pattern template, we recommend visiting the Salt glossary to familiarize yourself with terms we think will support your creation of patterns.
The template is built using the Salt DS figma library–its layout and presentation is also controlled by Salt’s variable modes (i.e., density).
Image 2: Installing Salt’s Spec Utilities library for access to the template
Before filling out the template, we advise defining and organizing your patterns in a dedicated Figma Project.
The patterns can either live within a single file or be documented in their own individual files.
In either case they should be kept within a single Project in your Team space.
For example, “Salt Design System” > “Patterns” > “Preferences Dialog pattern”.
The Figma ‘group ID’ for the Project is required to register and display your patterns with Salt’s Business Pattern Index.
This avoids interference or confusion with other, unrelated files.

found that for the first time in 6 years, web accessibility is getting

title: Demystifying Touch Density
content: In today's digital landscape, creating a seamless user experience across various devices is crucial.
Responsive design is the key to achieving this, and one of the essential elements in responsive design using Salt is understanding and implementing touch density (TD) effectively.
In this blog post, we'll explore how to use touch density in responsive design to enhance user experience.
Density refers to how much content can fit on a screen based on the size and spacing of components.
It is a foundational aspect of the Salt Design System, ensuring that all components, spacing, and typographic elements align proportionately.
: Designed for mobile and tablet devices with larger touch targets that meet DAKB accessibility criteria.

Responsive design adapts layouts to various screen sizes and orientations using multiple breakpoints, typically from Extra Small (XS) to Extra Large (XL), to accommodate mobile, tablet, and desktop devices.
The aim is to ensure content remains readable and accessible, enhancing the user experience by allowing layouts to adjust fluidly across different devices.
: On desktops, any density can be used depending on the content.
This flexibility allows designers to choose the most appropriate density for the specific needs of the application, whether it's data-heavy or content-light.
: For these devices, using touch density is recommended.
Touch density is designed to ensure optimal touch targets, making it easier for users to interact with the interface using their fingers.
The touch density ramps (spacing, type, size, etc) all follow the same scaling rules as other densities.
Its primary purpose is to meet the firms accessibility obligations–specifically min-touch size at 44px–it isn't designed for any one particular device.
When using touch density out the box, consider the nuances of the device that you're designing for (i.e., desktop, tablet, mobile).
This is typically not a consideration for smaller densities.

For example, a desktop screen has more space available and will easily accommodate the TD H1 typestyle or —spacing-300 token, whereas mobile is far more space constrained and may be better suited to a smaller heading or spacing token.
How to Effectively Use TD on Smaller Screens
To effectively use touch density on smaller screens, consider the typography and spacing tokens that you use.
We recommend that in mobile breakpoints (S, XS), smaller Display and Heading typography  is used.
This ensures that font sizes are appropriate for smaller screens.
For example, if you are using LD and H1 typography  tokens for desktop screens (XL, L, M), use TD H2 typography  tokens for tablet and mobile (S, XS).
If you are using the H1 component this can be achieved by setting
when a smaller screen is detected.
Display1 from the LD type ramp on desktop screens should be Display2 from the TD type ramp on mobile for the best visual result.

This only applies for Heading and Display typestyles, other type styles, such as body, action, and notation, use the same tokens across all breakpoints, with only the density changing on mobile devices.
When designing responsive layouts, for accessibility purposes it's crucial to switch to touch density for mobile devices, regardless of the density used on desktop screens.
In mobile breakpoints (S, XS), we recommend reducing the spacing for margins, gutters, and padding to make the most of the limited screen real-estate.
Salt recommends typically using Spacing 300 for desktop across any breakpoint.
This should change to Spacing 200 on tablet and Spacing 100 on mobile.
If you’re using Spacing 200 on desktop, continue to use Spacing 200 on tablet and changes to Spacing 100 on mobile.
Lastly, Spacing 100 on desktop stays the same as Spacing 100 on tablet and mobile.
By using these spacing values, Salt ensures the best visual results on mobile devices, affecting margins, gutters, padding between components and content, and the padding of container components.
Be sure to assign the correct spacing tokens in both Figma specs and in code.
To help you implement layout correctly in your builds you can use our padding and gap props on our layout component and refer to our
For practical examples, you can refer to the
Effectively using touch density in responsive design is essential for creating a seamless and accessible user experience across different devices.
By understanding density and breakpoints, and making device specific decisions about typography and spacing, designers can create interfaces that are both functional and visually appealing.
Whether you're designing for mobile, tablet, or desktop, keeping touch density in mind will help you create a user-friendly interface that meets the needs of your audience.
