title: How Salt builds Figma components
content: Figma components tailored to the business
We often get questions about why Salt components are built a certain way–why some have inline editable parts, limited nesting, or are split into sets rather than variants.

This article explains the thinking behind Salt components and aims to help you use Salt components more confidently, and when needed, extend them or build your own patterns in ways that remain efficient, consistent, and aligned with code.
Core principles for Figma component construction
as possible, balancing designer experience with Figma document performance.
To do this, we approach component construction with three key principles in mind:
: Striving to maintain low memory usage and layer counts, whilst ensuring components are easy to discover in the Assets panel and 'Swap instance' dropdown.
: Instead of rigid, one-size-fits-all components, we design parts that can be assembled into larger UI structures.
This reflects how components are implemented in code.
: Business use cases vary, and we build flexibility into our library to
to be built that have different requirements.
: We split variants into separate component sets for performance and clarity when variations diverge in purpose or structure.
This maintains lightweight components and helps to reduce overall size and memory usage of your design documentation.
For example, Date Picker components are split into separate sets since single and range pickers have distinct use cases.
In turn, this separation aids in discovery when searching or browsing for components in the Assets panel and 'Swap instance' menus.
6/6/25 Note: The Salt DS Figma library variables significantly reduce the number of variants we need to build.
With this in mind, we are starting to consider which component sets are appropriate to merge into single components without impacting your documentation.
Utilizing components and component sets instead of variants
: We limit component nesting and use the minimum number of viable, uniquely named layers.

This keeps memory use to a minimum, ensures component structure is easy to understand/ copy, and ensures component props and overrides are reliable and persist (a known issue when swapping between components and variants with nested compone
: Some Figma components contain smaller component parts that can be changed.
For example, the Salt DS Figma Form Field is constructed of component parts for:
Label: Consists of top, left placed labels.
Form control: Input types, checkbox, radio groups.

This is a Figma limitation with components – it is not possible to repeat elements inside a component.
For example, changing row and column numbers will not work unless the template is detached.
Detaching has no impact on the template itself; all parts remain linked to the library.
We only componentize the template because there is no other distribution method in Figma.
Why should you care about the 'text' elements in a cell?
By design, the plugin does not consider the cell type in the body of the grid.
This keeps the plugin flexible and extendable.
Regardless of the cell type you choose, if it contains a text element, the plugin can provide it with data.
This also means you can create your own custom cell types and swap them into the grid.
These cells will also work with the plugin!
Why can't I see my columns and rows?
By default, the bounding box of the grid clips the grid’s content; this means you can scale a grid to fit a specific area within your application.
If your grid does not appear to change size, grab the bottom right-hand resize handle and drag the bounding box to increase its height and width.
Why do my new columns and rows look different?
As mentioned in ‘Why should you care about 'text' elements in a cell?’, the plugin does not detect specific cell types in the grid body.
This means that when you add rows or columns, the cells that are added will default to a standard type.
Follow the instructions in the video to quickly update these cells to the required type.
Do I need to use the templates?
No, although using the templates is a great starting point for anyone looking to create a grid quickly that is editable with the support of the plugin, you are not obliged to use them.
There is an alternative method which allows you to create a grid from scratch using the plugin – the details of which have been highlighted in the Data Grid Figma guides.
Why do not all templates include column groups and floating filters?
Grids containing column groups and floating filters are intended to be used as a convenient starting point if your design requires either of these grid features.
The video tutorial explains the ideal workflow for configuring these.
How do I configure grid cell types?
Check out our handy Figma guides, which go in depth on how to configure different cell types within a grid.

“What should I do before running a library update so nothing breaks or resets?”
Before updating, confirm your file’s Theme and Mode in the Properties panel and switch to the correct option for your setup (JPM Brand, Legacy (UITK), or Chase).

title: Salt DS Figma Libraries
content: The new Salt DS Figma library cover pages

Designers will know that Salt has multiple Figma libraries which support different themes–those supporting UITK styles built before Figma released variables in early 2024, and those supporting JPM Brand styles which benefit from the improve
In total there are 13 libraries...too many.
Pre- and post-variable libraries aren’t compatible with each other and navigating so many libraries is inefficient and creates complexity.
For the start of 2025, Salt has released a new Salt DS Components and Patterns Figma library–reducing the total libraries from 13 to 6.
Your migration to the Salt DS libraries will depend on which of the existing libraries you are using and whether you are using Salt components directly or through a
(such as Pepper, MTK, Navigator, CRUX, UniversalDS, etc).
Previous libraries are now marked as retired and will no longer receive updates.
From the start of 2025, only Salt DS Figma libraries will be updated.
We will leave the existing Light/Dark Figma Libraries (non-variable based, UITK themed) published until
, and the Salt (Next) Libraries (variable based, Brand themed) until
We recommend planning your migration to the new Salt DS libraries before these dates.
The Salt DS libraries will be the single source of truth that Salt maintains moving forward.
You can start using them now.
If unsure, please first ask your
, or reach out to the team.
Please review the following migration guides.
If you need help after migrating, we’re happy to lend a hand:
Migration guidance from Salt Light, Dark libraries
Why have we made this change?
It's important to state, with this update
the design of the components and patterns are not changing
, there are no changes to Salt's code.
This update will streamline design processes for Salt design consumers and the Salt Design Team.
Ease of migration and library set up
: The new components support both UITK (Legacy) and JPM brand themes.
There is no longer a need to install multiple libraries.
Simply change swap between the two themes and see components instantly update.
If you’re using the UITK (Legacy) theme to migrate a UITK application, this theme capability will enable you to instantly swap your designs to the JPM brand theme once your migration is complete.
: The new library aligns to Figma's best practices–supporting both themes with drastically reduced instances and tax on Figma's memory.
Alignment to JPM brand and simplified theme selection
: No longer a need to set multiple styling options to define the brand theme–it comes configured out-the-box, and provides a platform to grow the brand identity for improved digital applications.
: With clearly defined themes out-the-box, design leads only need to direct teams to a specific theme and ensure development partners are informed of the appropriate theme to reference.
: Fewer libraries for the Salt design team to manage and update means we can ensure the quality of the libraries and spend more time on features for app delivery teams.
: With fewer libraries to manage, the component and pattern creation times will be reduced.
Documentation and QA testing will also be more efficient as themes, modes and densities can be switched easily within the same library.
In addition to reducing the number of libraries, we are also simplifying the number of variable (styling) options.
This means the Salt themes are now available out-the-box and easier to pick from.
The same themes are achieved in code using the
The two themes of the Salt Design System: Legacy (UITK) and JPM Brand
We're achieving this by combining the 'styling options'.
In the Salt (Next) Figma library these options provide 128 possible styling combinations.
In the Salt DS library, we've reduced the options down to three: Theme, Mode and Density.
This reduces the possible combinations to just 16.
Simplified theme selection in the new Salt DS Figma library

Designers using any Light, Dark or Next Salt libraries directly
Business Libraries that provide reusable domain specific Business Patterns that are built on Salt Light, Dark or Next Figma components

title: Salt DS migration FAQs
content: Welcome to the Salt DS Migration FAQs!

title: Build Business Patterns
content: A Business Pattern Library, or Business Library, is a collection of common UI patterns for a given domain (i.e., a line of business, organization, platform) that application delivery teams can use in production builds and design specificati
These business patterns combine Salt components and tokens with business logic and data to create reusable solutions which solve for specific business tasks of application users.
Image 1: Salt Business Library model courtesy of Sam Hampton (Markets Design ED)
Delivery teams can compose multiple business patterns together (alongside Salt components) using Salt Layout components and/or
tokens to create UIs for each capability within an application.
The following video, created by Alastair Mack (Securities Services Design ED) illustrates this experience stack:
: Combo Box combined with Salt Form Fields to create…
: Filter Bar composed with Charts and Data Grid to create…
: Transactions Viewer connected with related capabilities to create…
Video 1: A video explanation of the Business Libraries model and UI experience stack provided by Alastair Mack, Securities Services Design ED
Video 2: Watch Richard Salaman, Digital Markets Design Lead, demonstrate the value of Business Libraries in Figma
Typically, a Business Library provides UI patterns for tasks in a specific domain.
However, these same or similar tasks may exist in other domains.

A Salt-based Business Library therefore presents an opportunity to share patterns not only within a single domain but across domains in the CIB, increasing the consistency of solutions implemented for clients and employees of the firm.
A great example of this is the reuse of the
Whilst MTK caters to applications in the Markets business, a quarter of their library is used across other domains, including Treasury, Securities Services and Post Trade.
Image 2: Salt-based Business Libraries sharing patterns across single and multiple domains
The benefits of a Business Library
A Business Library doesn’t need to be an expensive investment.
It can mature as much as budgets, resources and timescales allow.
The goal is to establish patterns that can be reused and scale the benefits of the design system:
Cost savings: Reduced design and development time with consistent quality
Faster time to market: Reduced product development lifecycles with reduced rework for faster releases
Improved collaboration: Increased time available for problem solving and pooled resources across domains
Brand endorsement: Increased trust in UI builds that leverage the strength of the
A Business Library can be as simple as a collection of design patterns in a Figma file or a technical solution with reusable code artifacts and published documentation.
to better understand the impact of a Business Library.
How Salt architecture supports Business Libraries
Salt’s predecessor, the UI Toolkit (UITK), was
to standardize CIB user interface design and development in an application landscape with diverse visual design identities.

It was successful in its goal to create a centralized library of accessible components that delivery teams could "drop" into their applications to accelerate delivery, with adoption in ~19,000 repos across all LOBs.
As UITK matured, so did app team UI delivery models.
Teams began creating local libraries combining design system components with business logic to create reusable business components for their portfolio of applications.
The problem, however, was that UI Toolkit wasn’t built to support this model.
Underlying dependencies, component-level styling, large components and opinionated APIs meant components were often broken, overwritten or duplicated.
Salt is built for domains to extend
Salt learned from these friction points
and is built to support business patterns by incorporating several key principles and features that facilitate flexibility, scalability and consistency.
We know we can’t build components for every use case across every line of business, so we focus on building small, high-quality, flexible
and then demonstrate how to put them together as
These patterns serve as a starting point for app experiences: use them as they are or add to / remove from them to tailor them to your use case.
Importantly, they aren’t restricted to opinionated APIs.
This distinction provides Salt with the flexibility required to build and support business patterns using Salt components and tokens.
We looked at the friction points of legacy APIs to make them more consistent and composable.
Salt components have features for the most common use cases.
For more nuanced use cases, their composable API allows you to control the elements with which they’re composed.
For example, Salt’s Form Field component can be displayed with any Salt form control or a custom control.
Image 3: Business pattern support using Salt’s composable API, demonstrated with Salt’s Form Field component
Both our React and Figma libraries follow this approach, enabling you to easily control the content of your components.
Figma has more restrictions than React, so we enable composition in Figma through:
: Predefined Figma components that can be dropped in from the Salt DS Figma library, configured and then detached
: Elements inside Salt DS Figma components that can be swapped for custom content
Salt’s technical components can be styled with one of
: the JPM Brand or Legacy (UITK) theme.
Salt themes enable delivery teams to streamline the process of creating a consistent design language across their business domain, platforms or products.
These themes are driven by Salt design tokens, created as an abstracted layer of CSS variables.
Tokens link components together by their
(i.e., by common purpose or intent), with neither 3rd party libraries such as MUI nor JSS dependencies.
It’s possible to use these tokens to optimize your design language for your application and users.
Want to make your Card components more discreet?
Creating and documenting business patterns doesn’t have to be difficult.

A Business Library need not be expensive, and Salt can help to create and maintain one at low cost.

Extend Salt's Business Pattern Index so it indicates commonly used or best-in-class assets.
Salt's Business Pattern Index will initially support 3 types of sources.
Each source identifies a list of shared components or design patterns and appears as an entry in Salt's Business Pattern Index.
Through the list entry, the User is able to navigate back to the shared content.
For each source, the content we pull is typically owned by a single product or owner.
As such, we can derive additional metadata to associate with the shared content.
For example, we could pull all shared stories from Markets Toolkit's existing Storybook and add metadata:
All stories pulled from the Markets Toolkit stories could then be filtered by, querying by

title: Value of Salt Business Libraries
content: A driving factor for creating Salt was to support the increasingly systematic delivery of applications within the firm.

By creating a Business Library of patterns, Application Delivery (AD) teams are creating a single source-of-truth which allows them to scale reusable UI patterns consistently across their platforms and applications and generate cost savings
Image 1: Salt Business Library model (Credit: Sam Hampton)
Salt’s predecessor, the UI Toolkit, wasn’t setup to support Business Libraries effectively.
Components were too large, too inflexible, too opinionated and contained hardcoded styles.
Because of this, the bar to contribution was seen as too high, leading teams to ‘do their own thing’ and not able to take full advantage of the design system.
Fast forward to Salt, and we took the active decision to lean into Business Pattern libraries by providing:
Small, compositional components and flexible patterns
–you can do far more with the system than meets the eye.
–the look-and-feel of Salt’s technical components can be optimized for users and use cases.
Documentation templates and a zero governance contribution platform–allowing teams to promote their great work via

We’re working with a number of

Image 3: Top-left clockwise, MTK (Markets), Universal (CDAO), CRUX (Cross Risk), Pepper (Global Banking), Navigator (Payment Operations) Business Libraries
By supporting Business Pattern libraries, Salt is helping to contribute further cost-savings and efficiencies to production frontend UI within the Commercial and Investment Bank (CIB).
We can illustrate potential cost savings for a Salt-based Business Library:
With a Business Library, AD teams can reuse Salt components and patterns to significantly reduce time needed to build a new feature or interface.
: A typical UI component (e.g., a button or dialog) takes 10 hours to design, code, test, and implement, but with a Business Library this time can be reduced to 2 hours for integration.
A Business Library ensures that design and implementation are consistent across a domain, reducing the likelihood of rework due to inconsistencies.
: Inconsistencies or rework typically consume 10-15% of a project’s total effort.
Assume a project of 1,000 development hours
and 10% savings due to consistent UI = 100 hours saved.
With ready-made Business Library patterns, AD teams can shorten product development cycles, allowing products to be launched faster.
This has the potential for faster revenue generation.

: If an application is developed 10-20% faster due to the use of reusable business patterns, and a typical software project takes 6 months to complete, a Business Library could save up to one month of development.
Assume one month of faster time-to-market leads to an opportunity cost saving of $50,000
A Business Library can scale Salt’s brand-endorsed JPM theme across the CIB.
The creates experiences for clients and the firm’s employees that are consistent with and familiar to the firm’s digital and physical touchpoints
: Consistency with brand presentation across all platforms can generate a 23% increase in revenue(*).
Assume a one month revenue generation of $50,000 for a given application

With a Business Library there is less back-and-forth about how patterns should look or behave since they are using Salt components.
This improves team collaboration and reduces delays.

Once a Business Library is built, future projects can use the same business patterns and reduce development time for new apps or updates.

These examples are only illustrative but demonstrate the potential value of Salt-based Business Libraries for the CIB.

title: Harnessing usability testing to bridge gaps
content: In October, I attended Lisa Fraser’s full day of in-person usability testing training session for tech professionals at the Bank St office.
I would highly recommend this UK-based training for all tech roles and experience levels.
An astonishment report is an onboarding reflection aimed at new joiners that asks them to write what surprised them most after joining the team or company.
Conducting this within the first 8 weeks is crucial to capture first impressions before the organization's culture shapes them.
Formative evaluation encourages users to think-aloud while completing assigned tasks.
This is preferable during the early stages of product development when you want to gather qualitative feedback to improve designs.
Summative evaluation, on the other hand, involves users performing tasks without providing ongoing feedback which helps to assess the overall effectiveness of the designs.
Scenario based testing is encouraged to set imagined yet realistic circumstances.
By doing so, users are better prepared to handle real-world challenges.
For example, "you are x user trying to accomplish y goal."
Avoid using exact terminology found on the interface in the scenario description as this could affect the results.
When possible, moderated testing is preferred to reduce bias and enhance the "think aloud" process.
While one person observes and takes notes, a moderator asks questions.
In the context of Salt, this would be preferable when introducing a major breaking change, for example with component behavior.
The minimum sample size for testing to have practical significance is 5.
Testing with 5 users in any given cohort tends to uncover about 85% of the most obvious usability problems.
Before users attempt a task, ask them what they expect to see to reveal gaps between anticipated and actual results.
This is a great way to measure task difficulty and learn users’ preconceptions.
We aim to integrate regular testing into all our processes, particularly the ongoing site re-design.
As I’ve been working on this, I plan to apply these insights to improve our testing methods.
In the meantime, we're temporarily restructuring pages to enhance communication.
For feedback or suggestions on the Foundations section of the external site, reach out through the usual support channels.
If you're interested in getting involved in testing, please feel free to contact me directly.

title: Salt team onboarding experience from a new joiner’s point of view
content: I recently joined the Salt design system mid-year as a designer and want to share my experience onboarding to the team as someone with very little to no experience with design systems (DS).
Regularly reflecting on your team’s process as a designer is important in driving change and innovating new ways of working, particularly when the team highly welcomes feedback.
Naturally, onboarding to any DS can be overwhelming, time consuming, daunting and fatiguing.
Hopefully by sharing some of my experience, this process can be made easier for everyone involved!
: Salt has evolved from UITK to Salt now towards Salt Next.
Migration from UITK to Salt is a multi-year effort that allows us to better serve models while Salt Next offers theming capabilities on top of the existing Salt libraries.
: It’s helpful to have an assigned buddy + manager to provide guidance through each onboarding step.
: All employees have access to the Salt DS Figma libraries at any time to view templates, documentation and WIP.
: In Salt, key members have key roles and responsibilities which helps to reduce the ambiguity surrounding who does what.
Despite a new job being structured, it can also feel unstructured at first.
Thinking like an owner and trying to figure things out yourself first helps.
: DS teams use ample internal naming conventions and abbreviations in their ways of working that can be hard to grasp.
: Exposure to large amounts of documentation at once located in different places and maintained in different formats is confusing.
: Migration plans mean that people within DS teams may be on different pages and can lead to inconsistencies surrounding how knowledge is passed on.
How can we improve the experience?
Everyone is busy, yet very excited to get to know you.
Other people’s busyness should not prevent you from finding your role in the team and asking for help when needed.
: A step-by-step onboarding process formatted in asynchronous videos, live sessions or onboarding documentation.
This can offer digestible one-size-fits-all tutorials such as how to enable Figma libraries, how to use plug-ins, a glossary of DS terms.
: Implement a guided weekly or monthly onboarding learning plan for new joiners to follow in order of priority.
This can cater to users’ needs based on their previous experience with DS or new role requirements.
: Continue to encourage team to learn by doing with users who are implementing the DS or with other DS within the company.
Current steps to improve the experience
Moving forward, we will continue to cater to these suggestions and are already expanding our onboarding content.

title: 2 weeks, 20 external participants - partnering with DXD research
content: In Q4 of 2024, Amrita Desmet partnered with a member of the XD research team to conduct an external unmoderated test on UserTesting.com.
This covered the foundations section of the external facing Salt site, specifically the Typography and Color page.
In total, the test took 1 sprint to conduct including scoping, creating and deploying the study.
Addressing the content gaps head on with user testing is a great way to further understand next steps and create an impactful test-and-learn method that’s highly repeatable.
Learn if users can navigate to the foundations section of the external site.
Learn if users understand content on the Typography and Color foundation page.
Gather general feedback to best formulate page content and design.
The study included task driven exercises that were think-out-loud with supporting short written questions to assess a user’s understanding of specific pages.
A participant screener filtered the correct user group type: 20 participants who work in tech or financial services and are based in the US or the UK.
Each participant's session was recorded externally through the UserTesting.com interface which records both the screen and face to measure overall sentiment.
The most common words used to describe the content on the pages was informative, clear and easy to understand.
The participants feedback can be broken down into categories:
Pain point: The location of foundations isn't intuitive and it’s difficult to find information.
Quote: “I had to dig it out.” (referring to locating the Typography page)
Pain point: General confusion about the site’s navigation structure.
Quote: “I'm a little confused about what the site does or how you use it.” -> Need for clearer IA structure.
Pain point: Mismatch between user’s mental model (expectation) and site’s IA (reality).
Quote: “I was under the impression that maybe under getting started you would have the equivalent of this foundations… like a step-by-step guide.”
Pain point: When lost, users revert to the search functionality to find information.
Quote: “When I can't find something straight away, I just use search feature.” -> Users used both the search bar and Command F function to locate key words.
Positive feedback: Positive sentiment around visuals and effects.
Quote: “The page is slightly more attractive 'cause it's got embedded pictures.”
Pain point: Inconsistent layouts caused aversion or confusion.
Quote: “It’s hard to read because of the way it’s formatted but the content is good.”
Positive feedback: Overall, content is digestible and text is easy to understand.
Pain point: Desire for more practical application and guidance examples.
Quote: “I think it would be helpful if it gave some examples of each.”
We have since identified opportunities for quick wins and are currently applying the feedback to drive improvements.
Conduct regular user testing to gather continuous feedback – user testing will continue in Q1 2025.
Optimize layout consistency across pages – new site templates will ensure a clear design language for our new site.
Improve navigation clarity – the Salt site’s IA has recently been changed to consider.
Enhance visual appeal with interactive elements.
Incorporate comprehensive visual examples for guidance.
With the help from the XD research team, Salt can now deliver more wholistic design decisions and form our own test-and-learn approach.
If you would like to be an internal participant in Salt's future testing, please reach out to Amrita as your insights are invaluable.

title: Design Lessons from Monzo - Insights for Salt's Design Systems
content: In February, Amrita attended an external event titled ‘Designing Monzo’ at the Monzo HQ in London.
The event included Monzo speakers covering topics such as designing with emotional intelligence at Monzo and scaling their design system.
Monzo’s goal with their design, in general, is to spark joy.
Money can evoke a range of emotions—anxiety, stress, fear.
Monzo addresses this by asking its customers, “How does this make you feel?”
and tailoring their services to help people change their association with their personal finances.

An interesting statistic during one of the talks mentioned "one in three people would rather scrub their toilet bowl than check their savings account," according to the VP of Marketing at Monzo, based on research conducted by the company.
JPM differs in that Salt offers a comprehensive range of components that can be applied across all varying application use cases in the LOBs of the investment bank.
We offer best-in-class business patterns for our digital experience stakeholders such as Payments and Markets.
How does Monzo’s DS team compare to Salt?
Monzo’s DS team consists of 4 people: 1 designer, 1 front-end developer, 1 back-end developer and 1 developer who covers everything else.
The company has grown from 6 designers in 2020 to 33 designers in 2025 with about 2-3 developers per designer.
This contrast in team size highlights how Salt, with our ~15 person team, benefits from a broader range of expertise and resources.
Currently, Salt has 8 designers and 6 developers in addition to receiving help from the design operations, content design and user research teams.
This enables us to support a mature DS that caters to the complex needs of a larger organization, while Monzo's lean team structure allows for rapid iteration in a more focused environment.
The Monzo DS team actively encourages their designers to break out of the DS constraints if they want to develop designs that spark more joy.
One notable example of this is their gamified in-app “1p savings challenge” experience.
This campaign is designed to encourage anyone to start saving a penny a day, which accrues over the year to save £667.95.
Over 1.2 million people in the UK have signed up for this program.
Monzo's 2023 rebrand experience highlights the importance of synchronizing efforts between brand and design system teams.
When the rebrand was announced on X, overnight, they received hundreds of customer comments pointing out that their in-app experience still looked the same - “Why hasn’t it changed?”
and “Did you really have a rebrand?”
Announcing a rebrand without having updated the app led to high levels of confusion.
This misalignment caused confusion and resulted in the DS team allocating 2 sprints frantically updating every component to match the new brand announcement.
In contrast, Salt prioritizes clear, frequent communication with our stakeholders, especially during JPM's recent firmwide rebrand.
We release a regular newsletter with product updates, which has garnered over 1,000 subscribers.
At the end of 2024, Salt also introduced Business Library Managers (BLMs) - individuals who oversee the use of Salt’s components within their respective LOB delivery teams.
This strategic initiative demonstrates Salt’s commitment to enhancing education and communication across CIB.
For more information on the BLMs, please refer to this product blog.

title: Transitioning to Salt - A case study with the Cybersecurity Design team
content: The Cybersecurity design team (CTC) is exploring the possibility of migrating to Salt.
With ~15 applications currently using Tuxedo, CTC is keen to understand the benefits of transitioning to Salt.
Amrita partnered with them to showcase the potential of Salt out-of-the-box through a set of example screens accompanied by comprehensive guidance.
This initiative aimed to help CTC learn what’s possible with Salt and make informed decisions about their future direction.
Side by side comparison of CTC in Tuxedo versus Salt
Amrita worked closely with the team following a systematic process:
: Understand the function or intent of the design (e.g. dashboard to communicate intra-day incident volumes).
Amrita dove into the existing CTC screens to find opportunities for greater consistency.
: Learn how Salt can be applied and engage in pattern identification for reuse.
Amrita shadowed a senior Salt designer to gain insights into his thought process and design approaches to help other teams migrate.
: Make executive design decisions on the optimal density, theme and mode for the product, testing various options.
Amrita provided 3-4 design options to demonstrate Salt's flexibility, showing how she built-up an evolution that CTC can follow.
: Develop a clear, actionable guidance spec that educates and enables CTC to reproduce the work independently.
Salt has a desire to document our approach so it can be recreated following a ‘learn one, do one, teach one’ strategy which Amrita provided.
How your team can recreate this
: Use screenshots of your existing designs to ensure all design files are tied to the new Salt library for consistency.
Try to avoid cross contamination of libraries whenever possible.
: Make sure you use Salt to its full potential.
If you’re unsure what’s available in Salt, visit our website and if you have further questions on migration, attend our bi-weekly office hours.
: Test different Salt densities, spacing, and standards to find the optimal solution for your team.
If you are detaching Figma instances, applying hex values for colors, or creating your own font styles you’re probably diverging from the system and making implementation in code more costly.
: Leverage the customization options within Salt to tailor the design system to your team's needs.
While system-imposed rules like density are fixed, self-imposed rules are malleable and can be adjusted to suit individual preferences, allowing for a tailored look and feel.
For example, a self-imposed rule might be the use of secondary banners throughout a design, or turning borders off for certain containers.
What Salt can do for you
Salt offers a range of benefits that can revolutionize your product – from flexible customization to light/dark mode adjustment at no additional cost.
Salt can help you empower your team to make informed decisions and gain a new wealth of knowledge.

The positive feedback from the CTC team highlights that '[The] work not only provides valuable assets that [we] can share with key decision-makers, but it has also been a tremendous learning experience for our design team.'
By capturing and disseminating the exploratory process with CTC, Amrita has laid the groundwork for a successful transition, potentially impacting ~15 apps.
We look forward to learning the outcome of their decision.
April 2025 outcome: CTC will be fully transitioning to Salt!

title: Understanding Duration in User Experience - Insights from the Salt Design System
content: The concept of duration plays a pivotal role in shaping how users interact with digital systems.
Duration refers to the time interval between a user's action and the system's feedback.
It is akin to motion, transition, or animation in other design systems, as it focuses on the timing and feedback of user interactions to enhance user experience.
Consistency in timing not only provides comfort but also fosters trust in a system.
The Salt Design System offers a structured approach to managing duration, ensuring that user interactions are both seamless and satisfying.
Detailed guidance on these response times can be found in the
, offering insights into how each duration type can be effectively implemented.
The Salt Design System categorizes duration into four distinct types: instant, perceptible, notable, and cut-off.
Each category serves a specific purpose in user interaction, providing designers with a framework to tailor system responses.

A key principle in user experience design is the Doherty Threshold, which posits that user experiences transition from frustrating to engaging when system feedback occurs in less than 400 milliseconds.
This principle emphasizes the importance of maintaining a balance between user awareness of the system's processing time and the feeling of control.
Users should perceive a slight delay, yet feel empowered by the system's responsiveness.
Perceptible delays, such as those experienced with tooltips and overlays, exemplify this balance.
) duration indicates that the system needs more time to process an action.
During a delay of 1 second, there is typically no need to provide visual feedback to the user; however, this duration can serve as a breakpoint.
Once the delay surpasses the 'notable' duration, it becomes beneficial to inform the user that the system is addressing the task.
component is an effective visual representation of a process that is taking an indeterminate amount of time to complete.
It can be displayed at any point between
, but should not be shown any sooner.
The assumption is that the user's actions will have completed before it becomes necessary to display a loading state.
By using a spinner or similar progress indicator, users are reassured that the system is actively processing their request, maintaining their engagement and trust.
In certain scenarios, systems may need to extend processing times beyond the cut-off point due to workflow dependencies.
For instance, a highly performant user interface might need to update numerous data points simultaneously.
In such cases, it's crucial to implement visual feedback that prevents system slowdowns and provides users with the necessary cues to navigate a complex UI environment.
When durations exceed the cut-off point, it's acceptable to extend them beyond 10 seconds, provided certain conditions are met:
The outcome doesn’t require immediate user input or response.
Users can shift their focus to other tasks during the extended duration.
The prolonged interaction is independent of, and does not impact, the time sensitivity of concurrent interactions.
In conclusion, understanding and effectively managing duration is essential for creating user experiences that are both intuitive and engaging.

By adhering to principles like the Doherty Threshold and leveraging the structured duration scale of the Salt Design System, designers can craft interfaces that not only meet user expectations but also enhance overall satisfaction.
If you have questions on duration, please feel free to reach out to the team for further clarification.

title: Salt Pattern Design Assets Naming Research
content: Aligning User Feedback with Final Definitions & Figma Distribution Mechanisms

To improve clarity, usability, and contribution in Salt Design System, we ran a research to refine Salt Pattern Figma design assets naming—aligning terminology with both consumer expectations and Figma's evolving capabilities.
Limitations in Figma: Salt can only publish assets as Figma components, restricting how patterns and examples are shared.
Need for Clear Distribution Mechanisms: Consumers require both components and pattern assets, each logically named and accessible.
Expectation Alignment: Existing terms like “stickers” are interpreted differently across teams.
We aim to introduce clearer terminology—especially for the two types of pattern assets—to better reflect their purpose and align with Figma’s evolving feature set.
Encouraging Contribution: Consumers wish to contribute examples (e.g., different examples of app headers and data grids).
The system must support this through intuitive terms and structure.
Most participants did not propose new names but generally agreed with terms “Templates” and “Stickersheets” for the 2 types of pattern assets.
Mixed feedback: Some prefer "Example Sheets" for clarity, while others associate "Sticker Sheets" with MTK/Vida and find them intuitive for internal reuse.
Consensus: Clear labelling and placement outside the main component library is crucial.
All participants primarily use the Asset Panel, rarely accessing the main file directly.
Discovery through patterns/templates should integrate with asset panel access, not hidden inside component libraries.
Confusion remains between patterns and components, especially for those new to design systems.
Some participants shared that people may mistakenly assume patterns = components, creating implementation mismatches with tech partners.
Group 1 (type 1: Componentized patterns): Perceived as clearer and more guided.
Something can be configured with more context for the designs.
Group 2 (type 2: Pattern examples): Seen as more complex and larger.
Often used as starting points, without the need to change.
As part of this work, we also discussed our asset naming approach with Figma team to ensure alignment with how Figma is evolving their own features—especially around templates and pattern sharing.
Figma’s suggestion reinforced our use of the term “Template” for assets that can be detached and customized, and “Stickersheet” as a starting point without requiring changes.
This helped validate our distinction between Component Templates, Pattern Templates, and Stickersheets.
The conversation also supported our goal of using names that:
Reflect how assets behave in Figma,
And remain flexible for future Figma updates (e.g., potential template-specific features).
Following the research findings, we've updated the Salt design assets naming in our Salt DS Components and Patterns.
You can find the details and the definitions of all Salt design assets in

Next, we will be creating a new Salt DS Pattern Stickersheets file—this will serve as a centralized space for all Salt DS stickersheets and make it easier for XD teams to explore, reuse, and contribute their own examples.

title: Design-Dev Handoff Survey Results
content: In our ongoing journey to refine and enhance the Salt Design System, we recently reached out to our community through an unmoderated remote survey.
Our goal was to gain a deeper understanding of the handoff process between design and development.
This survey was shared with users and potential users of Salt, specifically focusing on those in design and development roles.
Over the course of two weeks, from July 16 to July 25, we gathered valuable insights via the Salt newsletter and Teams.
We were thrilled to receive 78 responses, including 20 developers and 58 designers.
Our participants represented a diverse array of roles, such as VPs (38), Senior Associates (22), and Associates (8), and came from various lines of business like CIB (48), GB (11), and CT (10).
We truly appreciate the time and effort everyone put into participating, as your feedback is crucial in helping us improve the Salt design system.
The survey revealed several key insights into the current state of the design-to-development handoff process:
: Many designers are utilizing Figma features that are only accessible to developers with Figma Dev Mode.
However, a significant number of developers do not have access to Dev Mode, which limits their ability to fully engage with the design files.
While all developers surveyed had some level of Figma access, most reported having only View-Only access.
: The handoff process is often asynchronous and siloed, with live walkthroughs rarely mentioned.
In some cases, developers and designers do not even know each other, leading to a lack of communication.
Handoff deliverables are frequently passed via Jira, with designers using Figma specs and specific handoff files.
However, a large majority of developers only know the basics of Figma, and some rely on static screenshots as design deliverables.

: The main challenges reported by designers include a developer knowledge gap regarding both Salt and Figma, a lack of Dev Mode usage, and inconsistencies between what is designed and what is developed.
These issues are exacerbated by a siloed handoff process and a lack of clear Salt documentation.
Despite the challenges, the Salt Design System is recognized for its potential to bridge the gap between design and development.
Designers frequently create Figma specs and prototypes, and the use of Figma annotations is common, although not all developers have access to these features.
To better support our consumers, the survey highlighted two main areas for improvement:
: There is a need to bridge the gap between what is available in Figma for Salt and what is documented on the Salt website and codebase.
This will help ensure consistency and clarity in the handoff process.
: Improving Salt documentation is crucial to address the knowledge gaps identified in the survey.
Clear and comprehensive documentation will empower developers to better understand and utilize Salt components.
While there are challenges to address, the positive aspects of Salt and the willingness of our community to contribute to its improvement are encouraging.
Moving forward, we'll focus on bridging the gaps identified and enhancing our documentation to better support our users.
We're committed to continuous improvement and look forward to implementing these changes to enhance Salt for all its users.
We would like to extend our thanks to all survey participants for their valuable insights and feedback.
Additionally, we are grateful to our research partners for their support and collaboration in conducting and analyzing this survey.

title: Lessons from Cancara OS - Lloyds Design System event
content: In September, some designers in Salt attended
Design Evenings LDN: Scaling Design Systems for a Multi-Brand, Multi-Platform Future
, where the Lloyds Banking Group design system team shared how they’ve been driving one of the most ambitious design system (DS) transformations in UK finance.
Building on the rebrand talk previewed at Config 2025, they revealed how Cancara OS now powers 4 brands: Lloyd, Bank of Scotland, Halifax, MBNA.
Speaker on stage with Salt team members in crowd
The Salt team share our key takeaways:
The Lloyds DS team emphasizes their approach to scaling across 4 key areas: brands, target audiences, products, and platforms.
They’ve identified 5 essential pillars for running a successful design system: metrics, UI Library, code repository, documentation, and governance.
These 5 pillars are equally important to Salt DS, and we focus on them everyday in our own work.
Design system scale and target states slide
Much like Salt, Lloyds supports a multi-brand experience.
In Figma, they maintain distinct sets of Figma libraries for each brand and use the swap libraries feature to switch themes between brands.
In Salt, we currently support JPM Brand and Legacy (UITK).
Instead of duplicating work, Salt has built theme-switching capabilities using variables that let multiple brands share the same foundations.
We’ve adopted this method to reduce bloating and ensure scalability across products.
Current variations of Lloyds brands slide
Cancara OS manages 2,000+ tokens and 5,000+ assets (icons, pictograms, illustrations).
Token categories span border, background, semantic, local, and contrast - plus temporary tokens to help teams manage tech debt.
Interestingly, they’ve also introduced Native Token Picker, a token picker tool inspired by Atlassian’s, guiding consumers toward the right tokens through a survey-style UI.
For example, consumers could use LLM Suite.
Salt manages tokens and assets in a similar way, though at a much smaller scale.
While we don’t have a token picker tool, Lloyds’ approach offers inspiration for potential future enhancements.
Cancara OS built a dedicated token set for data visualization, separate from the main color ramp.
The set is light/dark mode compatible and WCAG compliant, supporting accessibility for color blindness.
Our team is working on building in Chart support in Q3/Q4 of 2025 following a similar approach, aiming to build on UITK charts with Highcharts.
We’re prioritizing accessibility and supporting multiple modes.
For Cancara OS, change requests come through a Confluence page or Design Clinics.
In Design Clinics, many designers receive valuable advice on their work.
Maintaining a strong relationship between the DS team and other designers is crucial.
The goal isn’t for the DS team to police, but rather to foster consistency and effectively disseminate guidance to all users.

Each is subject to a rigorous audit and review before being merged into the system.
Proposals without broad use cases are kept in local libraries, ensuring flexibility without overloading the system.

title: Building an Accessible Carousel for Salt Design System
content: In our latest sprint, the Salt team has moved the

This milestone offers an opportunity to reflect on why we built a carousel, the challenges we faced, and the importance of accessibility for this somewhat contentious UI element.
Salt Carousel has no accessibility defects and passed WCAG 2.1 AA
Carousels are widely used across our business, especially on landing pages where first impressions matter.
They allow us to showcase multiple pieces of content in a compact, visually engaging way.
Ignoring carousels doesn’t solve the business need.
Without a robust, accessible solution, teams would build their own—leading to inconsistent patterns, poor accessibility and misalignment with our brand guidelines.
Carousels are often criticized for their accessibility shortcomings, since they can create barriers for users who rely on assistive technologies.
Building an accessible carousel isn’t trivial.
Many carousels trap focus or make movement between slides very difficult.
Keeping tab order logical and predictable isn't easy.
Users may not know which slide is active, or how many slides there are.
Preventing automatic slide changes from disrupting users is important, especially when they interact with the carousel.

However, despite alternatives, carousels remain a popular design choice—especially on our stakeholder's homepages.
We considered building a carousel from scratch.
But not every product requires one.
In addition, there are excellent headless options available.

title: A guide to Salt versioning
content: Versions can be confusing and complicated to understand:
What is the latest version of Salt?
Which version should use in your project?
Will a new version impact your delivery?
Here, we break down the topic of versioning in Salt, to help you make informed decisions about your version updates.
In Salt, a version represents a new release of a code package within the design system.
Each release may introduce new components, features, styles or bug fixes.
Versioning provides clarity on the value and impact of each update, helping products to manage their own change.
It distinguishes between patch or bug fixes, minor updates with new features, and major releases that
require code changes to your product.
What version numbers mean for you?
Each Salt version is identified by a unique number, which serves as a reference for when updates were made.
Salt’s version number consists of 3 numbers, in the format of
The unique number that Salt uses follow an industry standard called "Semantic Versioning", often shortened to
To get most value from the design system, you should understand what semver means, how it impacts your delivery, and what you need to do to adopt it.
: Changes that break how things work in your end-user experience or how you create them in code, such change is referred to as a ‘breaking change’.
These changes can sometimes be costly, but in other cases, when removing legacy features, they may have little to no impact.
need to be changed to adopt the changes.
: Version adoption will need to be scoped and planned into your delivery roadmap–depending on the components affected, you may need more time to adopt.
: Addition of new features that can enhance the user experience.
: Updates are additive and provide you with more features and enhancements, while preserving existing functionality and compatibility.
They allow users to benefit from new capabilities without requiring additional code changes.
Regular adoption of minor releases will reduce the impact of future breaking change and reduce cost of updates.
Read release notes and changelogs to understand the value that can be added to your product by picking up minor releases.
Follow the recommended approach for removal of deprecate code/tokens, to minimize the future cost of any major change.
: Small, corrective updates that address bugs, security issues, or minor flaws in a product without altering its features or overall functionality.
: These changes improve stability and reliability, ensuring software continues to operate as expected without introducing new capabilities or breaking existing compatibility.
Update your code when each patch release is available to minimize defects in your product.
At the time of writing, Salt’s Core package
- has not made any major/breaking changes to Core –
Salt is still version 1 after 2 years
that's 51 releases of new components and features that did not require code updates to use
- has not yet made bug fixes for the latest release.
How do I know what each version contains?
Each Salt package has it's own Changelog that defines the latest version and describe the changes within the release.
Changelogs can be somewhat technical so a product view of change is provided, typically every sprint, through our Newsletter (
The latest version number and change details are always reported at the top of every newsletter.
Salt operates in two-week sprints, with a new minor or patch version typically
This approach ensures a continuous flow of value, allowing smaller changes to progress without being delayed by larger updates.
Typically, major releases are annual events, so will come with plenty of notice (at least 1 quarter) and documentation/tools to help with migration.
Patch releases can also be more reactive, made as-and-when required depending on the severity/impact of any issue.
Deprecation is the process of marking components, features or tokens as outdated, signaling they should be avoided and will be removed in future releases.
Sometimes, waiting for a major release isn’t practical.
To keep moving forward, we use deprecation: we announce that a component or token will no longer be supported, but it remains available until the next breaking change.
This approach allows teams to transition smoothly, ensuring applications continue to work while providing time to update to the new solution.

title: Using Figma deprecation to get the most from Salt DS
content: As Salt Design System evolves, we are continuously improving our Salt DS Figma libraries to ensure designers using the system can produce the best documentation for handover.
Early access to, and adoption of, new Figma features
Improvements to structure, naming, and styles
At the same time, we appreciate that designers use our libraries in live files, and that we need to be sensitive to the impact our updates could have on documentation and delivery timescales.
Our goal: App designers should never see unexpected change to their design documentation when they update Salt libraries.
To help achieve this goal we deprecate old Figma variables and components.
It’s a common process in application development.
When a feature is marked as ‘deprecated’ it means it is old and shouldn’t be used.
It signals the feature will be removed in the future (typically the next
) but until that time, it will remain available and there will be no change to the application.
A deprecated feature might be replaced by something new and improved.
In this case, you have the control to decide when you start using the new feature.
Figma isn’t good at giving you control over your updates.

When you get an update notification in your project, you can choose to accept updates or dismiss them, but the process can be slow and (even with release notes) lack enough information for you to make an informed decision—it discourages des
Image 1: Figma’s library update notification, complete with release notes
To reiterate our goal: You should never see unexpected change to your design documentation when you update Salt libraries.
Salt uses deprecation as a way for you to update libraries quickly with confidence that you can continue working uninterrupted; Nothing will change unless you allow it.
In simple terms, Figma deprecation keeps you up to date and gives you extra time to make changes when you’re ready.
This is what the Figma deprecation process looks like:
We consider an update to be breaking (it will result in an unexpected change to design files)—we preserve the current component but mark it as deprecated.
A duplicate component is made, and the update is applied to it.
Salt publishes the library update; Figma notifies designers and designers update their files.
The new component is available in the Assets panel, but design files do not change; The current component is indicated as deprecated.
At a convenient time, designers swap to (or start using) the new component.
At a point in time, the deprecation is removed from the library.
We avoid deprecation when a change:
fixes something broken (e.g., a style doesn’t match code and needs to be corrected)
is not visible by default (e.g., a new feature needs to be toggled on to see it).
How we indicate something is deprecated
When a component is deprecated, we clearly mark it in multiple ways to ensure visibility and awareness:
❌DEPRECATED – This will be removed in a future release
Let’s look at a Salt Overlay component update:
The description is updated with the deprecation notice
The new version appears with the NEW_ prefix
Image 2: Deprecation and update of Salt’s Overlay component
If you discover a deprecation after you update, it’s a signal that you should stop using that specific Figma asset and plan to update.
Deprecations are announced in Salt’s Figma
, including what’s changing and the release of the new version.
It often has improved structure, naming, and style use, and may support new Figma and/or plug-in features.
Our Figma library reflects the most up to date minor version of Salt (learn more Figma versioning in our
Your tech partner should do the same—a minor version release is additive and not a breaking change.
Discuss with your tech partner when you can use the NEW_ component and its new features.
Swap deprecated components with the new ones from the Assets panel or Swap Instance menu.
As much as possible, we will try to limit changes, but you may have to reapply overrides and props to the component once swapped.
If you’re unsure how to migrate, or need help understanding the change, please reach out to the team, we’re here to support a smooth transition.
Being proactive with deprecated components helps keep your design specs clean, up to date, and aligned with the latest improvements in Salt Design System.
How long you have to swap deprecations
Typically, you should expect the following timescales for different types of
| Figma variables                | Salt Figma variables closely align with our coded design tokens, and both are regularly reviewed to keep the system clean and efficient.
When a design token is deprecated in code, we do the same with the corresponding Figma variable | 3 sprints (6 weeks)                            |
| Figma components: Scenario 1   | A Salt component is deprecated in code, so the Figma equivalent is also deprecated.

It remains in the library until the next breaking code change (i.e., a Major version release—currently Salt is still in Version 1) | A major version update is considered a significant undertaking and will come with at least 1 quarters notic

| Figma components: Scenario 2   | A Salt component is only deprecated in Figma; it’s unrelated to a change in code (i.e., because of a Figma update or change to the structure of the Figma component) | 3 sprints (6 weeks)

| Salt’s Figma Templates         | Salt Template components are pre-built examples that help designers implement best practices—they demonstrate the recommended approach to putting components together.
They reflect the latest and greatest from Salt. | 3 sprints (6 weeks)                            |
| Salt Icons                     | In both code and Figma, we will not be deprecating icons, or country symbols, in the future.
These updates are considered fixes or necessary enhancements and will be rolled out automatically.
What happens if you don’t update
It’s important to note that when a deprecated thing is removed from a Figma library it won’t disappear from design files.
The integrity of your file is preserved.
However, since the asset no longer exists in the library, any instances that remain in your file will not receive future updates.
For example, a deprecated variable that has been removed from the library will not receive any new theme options or color changes.
to remove risk from your design documentation
to give you more control over your library updates
to enable iterative progress and improvement to Salt libraries
Remember, you must adopt the deprecation’s replacement in order to continue receiving library updates from Salt.
Finally, keep an eye on our
If there is a significant change that we need to notify you of, we will
post to these channels as soon as possible.

title: Introducing Salt Figma Design Assets - Components, Templates, and Stickers
content: Salt Figma design assets are reusable elements used to build user interfaces.

Each format is intentional and maps to how the Salt Design System is meant to be used in Figma—so teams can move quickly while keeping design documentation performance-friendly, composable, flexible, and aligned with coded implementation.
are reusable UI building blocks distributed as Figma components, intended to align with their corresponding Salt coded components (e.g., Avatars, Banners, Buttons).
are starter compositions served as Figma components.

They combine multiple Salt components and patterns into structures that can be configured and then detached for further customization (e.g., Checkbox group template, Form field template, Button bar pattern template, Wizard pattern template)
provide contextual examples or pattern references as Figma frames.
They offer practical starting points for specific use cases (e.g., Forms stickers, International address form stickers).
Why using Figma assets the right way matters
Using the right asset format and following its intended workflow helps:
keep Figma files lightweight and easier to work with
reduce rework and inconsistency across teams
stay aligned with Salt coded components where applicable
receive fixes and improvements through Salt library updates
Image 1 - The Banner components with configurable properties

when there is a Salt code component in core and the intended workflow is a reusable building block that teams can quickly configure via props, without requiring changes to its structure (e.g., adding an additional item).

In these cases, the Figma component should be entirely controllable from the props panel, allowing designers to configure it quickly and confidently, knowing it reflects the capabilities of the coded equivalent.
The Figma component should align as closely as Figma allows with the coded component’s props, behavior, and accessibility expectations to maximize design–code consistency.
A reusable Figma element (with commonly used purpose and generic interactions) with a corresponding coded UI building block exists in the source code (not a context-specific example).
Design differences can be achieved by setting props (e.g. variants, state, icons/labels) and swap/content area without detaching or restructuring.
Configure via props and instance overrides (including values and instance swap for custom content where relevant).
Don’t detach, so you can continue to receive updates to the foundational components.
Image 2 - The Form field component template with configurable properties and three Salt component instances (Label, Control, Helper Text) inside
for a repeatable starter composition (Salt components/patterns) that teams can configure quickly, then detach to customize structure.
Some templates have repeatable elements built into the equivalent coded component that we cannot reproduce in Figma without creating heavy components with hidden elements that are often unnecessary.
Templates support frequently used starter compositions that reduce rework and improve findability.
Image 3 - The Wizard pattern template with configurable properties
Insert the template, configure the baseline, then detach to customize the structure (add/remove/reorder elements).
After detaching, keep inner elements connected as Salt components where applicable (avoid detaching everything).
Image 4 - Examples of International Address Form pattern and International Phone Number Input pattern stickers
when the best way to share the solution is a more specific contextual example, rather than a foundational generic component/template.
Shows how Salt components can be constructed or configured for a specific use case or context, and not simply a generic element.
Best shared as a copyable example and reference layout, governing it as a single component/template would be too complex or too restrictive.
Copy the stickers as frames into your file and adapt as needed.
, stickers are not distributed as published components)

How to use Salt Figma Design Assets

title: How to use Salt Figma Design Assets (Components, Templates, and Stickers)
content: Salt Figma Design Assets – Components, Templates, and Stickers
, this article shows you how to use these Figma assets to create design specs efficiently and effectively.
| Figma Design Asset type | Purpose                                                                                                           | How to use

| Component               | Reusable UI building block with a corresponding Salt code component, configurable via props without restructuring | Configure via props and instance swap for custom content if needed

| Template                | Starter composition of components and patterns                                                                    | Configure via props first, then detach and customize the structure (e.g. add/remove/reorder elem
| Sticker                 | Contextual examples or pattern references                                                                         | Copy and paste to your file, and adapt as needed
Confirm you have the main Salt Figma libraries enabled: For setup instructions, follow:
Getting started: Designing with Salt in Figma
Components and Templates: Salt DS Components & Patterns Library (published library)
Stickers: Salt DS Stickersheets (shared Figma file, not published)
Image 1 - A Figma file with the main Salt Figma libraries (Salt DS Assets, Salt DS Components and Patterns, and Salt DS Themes) enabled
Using a Component means you start from a governed, code-aligned building block that stays connected to Salt library.
You can configure by setting properties, rather than creating the UI element from scratch.
Step 1 — Insert a component from Assets panel:
After Salt DS Components & Patterns Library is enabled, search or browse the component in the Assets panel and drag it onto the canvas.
Use the prop panel on the right (variants, size, state, hierarchy, with or without icons and labels etc.).
Update text value, and icon type if needed.
This captures most specific differences with minimal manual editing.
Step 3 — Use Swap instance where available if needed:
If you need custom content inside a component, use the Swap instance property to swap in your content via Salt’s Content area and Swap placeholders.
Many Salt components support this so you can customize content while staying connected to the library.
Image 2 - 2 ways to find the Button component – browse to Button component or search Button in the Assets panel
Image 3 - Examples of components with Content area and Swap (Input, Card, and Accordion)
Don’t detach components – detaching breaks the update path, increases manual rework when libraries change, and makes designs harder to keep consistent.
If you think you need to detach, check these first:
props, variants, and swap instance options
an existing alternative component/pattern in the library
A key Salt principle is safe upgrades.
Salt has Figma deprecation process to enable you stay up to date with library releases without breaking design files and seeing unexpected changes, learn more in
Using Figma deprecation to get the most from Salt DS
Templates reduce setup time for common structures.
Use Templates when you want a repeatable starter composition that teams can configure quickly, then detach to make structural changes.
Checkbox group: you can configure the orientation for the checkbox group with the relevant responsive setup, then detach to add more checkboxes as needed.
Form field: you can configure the label placement, the type of control, the state, and help text, then detach for further configurations as needed.
Step 1 — Insert a template from Assets panel:
Templates are published like components from Salt DS Components & Patterns Library.
Search or browse a template in the Assets panel and drag it onto the canvas.
Step 2 — Configure the baseline before detaching:
Use the template’s props to set the baseline first.
Step 3 — Detach to customize the structure:
Detach when you need to add/remove/reorder parts.
After detaching, keep inner Salt components connected where applicable (avoid detaching everything).
Image 4 - 2 ways to find the Form Field template – browse to Form Field or search Form Field template in the Assets panel
Stickers let you reuse a contextual example or pattern reference built with Salt as a starting point.
Copy them into your file and adapt them when the solution is context-specific and when you want to avoid assembling it from scratch.
Step 1 — Open Salt DS Stickersheets Figma file:
Browse Salt DS Stickersheets for stickers (as frames in different pages, not published components) to see if an example or reference fits your use case.
Some Salt components and patterns include links to the related stickers, you can search or browse the stickers in the Assets panel.
Drag it onto the canvas and check the description and links that direct you to Salt DS Stickersheets.
Step 2 — Copy frames into your file:
Copy the stickers and paste into your working file.
Step 3 — Adapt for your use case:
Update layout and content as needed, while continuing to use Salt components/variables where appropriate.
Image 5 - To find the International Address Form sticker – browse the list of pages or search International Address Form in Salt DS Stickersheets file
Image 6 - You can also search or browse the stickers in the Assets panel.
Drag it onto the canvas and check the description and links that direct you to Salt DS Stickersheets
Detaching breaks the update connection and increases inconsistency.
Salt provides props, variants, and swappable parts to reduce the need for detaching.
“Difference between a template and a sticker?”
Templates are more generic repeatable starter compositions; stickers are more context-dependent patterns expressed as examples.
“What if I can’t find what I need?”

Check Salt site documentation, the Salt DS Figma library and the Stickersheets file, if you still can’t find an asset that matches your use case, you can request an enhancement or contribute a business example sticker (built with Salt compo

title: 2025 Mobile roadmap
content: As adoption of Salt continues to increase exponentially across JPM, its use cases are expanding across LOBs, brands and channels.

One such use case is an increased demand for mobile experiences, in part accelerated by the new Global Banking business, and an increase in mobile use cases that were previously part of the Commercial Bank, but also due to increasing client
Several native and web mobile libraries already exist, supporting one or a few mobile applications.
These libraries are not aligned to CIB brand standards or Salt design standards.
With this growth, we recognize the need to evolve our design foundations and layouts so application teams can implement their native or web mobile preferences.
Our consumers need to be able to deliver client experiences through their chosen mobile solution, which meet these requirements:
They're consistent with their desktop solutions
They align to the JPMC brands
They're competitive with modern mobile experiences
Current state of Salt’s Touch Density
Salt has historically been a desktop-first design system, catering for business use cases.
Mobile experiences have been limited and significantly lower priority for CIB businesses.
enables delivery teams to build experiences that are optimized for the ‘data density’ of their application context on
Salt tokens follow a scaling system that makes them
as density changes from high to medium, low and touch—components and the space around them increase in size with density.
When applications are data dense and complicated High Density is applicable.
Low Density would be applicable for applications less frequently used by JPM clients.
Touch Density exists to enable teams to meet minimum touch accessibility obligations, but it’s
The scaling system presents challenges when touch is used on mobile (i.e., small screens).
There's an inherent contradiction—components and layout spacing is larger with touch density, while available screen space gets smaller with mobile devices.
Salt has documentation which explains how delivery teams can
resolve this contradiction for small screens
to deliver better mobile experiences with Touch Density, but a more robust, reliable and intuitive solution is required to meet business standards.
Despite the increased demand for mobile solutions, there currently is still not the demand for a centralized native mobile system from the business.
Delivery teams prefer to manage their own libraries/ implementations of native components, to ensure:
Ongoing delivery and ease of maintenance
Facilitate mobile experiences through design foundations and tokens that meet CIB’s mobile UI requirements
Document a point-of-view and guidance for how to use Salt to achieve native or mobile web implementations, with known limitations and realistic expectations
Ensure the compatibility of existing Salt web components with mobile devices and native OS accessibility configurations
to create and distribute a centralized mobile system.
However, a number of mobile systems already exist in CIB and are in scope to support the JPM Brand and Salt design standards.
These are included in our mobile roadmap below.
Limited mobile priorities in these quarters.
Mobile efforts in this quarter focus on publishing documentation which explains how to use Salt’s existing Touch Density more effectively for small screen experiences.
Salt will define the foundational values (i.e., size, spacing, corner) required for a dedicated Mobile Density, which will be:
The long-term replacement for the existing Touch Density
Comparable with native mobile UI design standards
, applicable to small screen touch devices, including Tablet and Foldable Mobile devices—broadly consistent with the
The mobile values will be made available to
in Figma as beta for testing and feedback.
Finalize the values required for a mobile density following this feedback and ensure they're in a ‘ready for dev’ state to implement into the Salt codebase in Q4.
There are three objectives in Q4.
Salt will partner with colleagues in DP Mobile to implement and deploy a series of test applications to iOS and Android environments.
This collaboration will test a number of implementation scenarios, all deployed as native (iOS and Android) applications:
: Uses Salt components directly—to identify and resolve existing mobile compatibility issues.
: Uses Salt components, tokens and layouts directly—to test a responsive experience from desktop web, reducing to mobile web, using a combination of breakpoints and device detection.
: Uses Salt tokens to style native components—to identify styling limitations and realistic expectations when adopting the JPM brand standards via Salt styles.

: Uses a mix of Salt components and native components to deliver applications aligned to Salt but benefiting from existing native mobile patterns—to understand the styling delta between deployed Salt and native components, both aligned to t
The goal of these test applications is to:
QA and ensure the compatibility of existing Salt web components with mobile devices.

This doesn't mean Salt will build mobile UI patterns, but rather ensure that existing components work on a mobile device (i.e., are bug free and function with a finger/thumb interaction) and respond to native accessibility settings.
Further test (and where necessary, update) the new Mobile Density values in Salt’s coded components.

Publish documentation to the Salt site (as a contribution and collaboration from DP Mobile) which guides consumers creating both native and mobile experiences, providing detail of limitations, realistic expectations and technical guidance.
The goal of this objective is to:
Release the Mobile Density, including any newly identified tokens required for mobile delivery) to the Salt codebase and Salt DS Figma libraries.
Publish a clear migration guide from Touch Density to Mobile Density.

Update Salt foundation documentation (i.e., Density and Responsiveness docs), in addition to any documentation referencing Touch Density) to provide clear guidance for the design standard and how it should be used in the design of mobile (a
Objective 3: Story DS Mobile component migration

The goal of this objective is to work with our Pepper Patterns partners in the Payments business to assist in the migration of their StoryDS mobile components to the Salt JPM Brand and Mobile density.
: This objective is dependent on the roadmap, strategy and capacity of our Payments partners.
Unless otherwise determined as a business priority with clear directives (or finalizing any incomplete efforts from the 2025 Mobile roadmap) there are no known goals for ‘Mobile’ in Salt in 2026.
