title: 2024 Themes
content: As we continue to develop our components and engage with more stakeholders, we have recognized the need to make some breaking changes to establish a solid foundation for theming.
These changes would significantly alter the structure of our palette layer and further differentiate the default Salt theme from UITK.

While this may pose challenges for adoption, it is necessary to address two conflicting stakeholder priorities: the gradual adoption of UITK styling for backward compatibility and the desire for a distinct visual identity and improved acces
To accommodate these priorities, we will maintain two themes and introduce the necessary mechanics and documentation to support theming.
This approach allows us to provide options for both gradual adoption and customization, ensuring that our design system can meet the diverse needs of our stakeholders.
Salt primarily focuses on delivering UITK parity and facilitating migration.
It is important to note that creating your own custom themes using the current version of Salt is not recommended.
This is because updates to components may potentially break any custom theme CSS overrides implemented by application teams.
At present, Salt does not have an agreed public API for styling that would mitigate this risk.
We are gradually releasing a unified color palette and introducing additional theme options, such as rounded corner support, accent color mapping, and heading typography mapping.
It's important to note that these additions will not cause breaking changes for teams that are not utilizing these specific features.
We will be publishing Salt 2.0 to support stable theming.
For teams looking to migrate, here are a few considerations:
If you are using vanilla Salt "out of the box," no changes are required.
If your Salt 1.0 theme was customized, either at the palette layer or by re-assigning variables, the overrides may not be compatible with Salt 2.0.
In such cases, a re-write of the customizations will be necessary.
Please note that theming in Salt 1.0 is not recommended.
If you have customized the Salt characteristics layer using hardcoded values, it is still possible to do so with Salt 2.0.
However, teams should consider transitioning to a more holistic approach provided by Salt 2.0's theming support.
In the future, we plan to publish off-the-shelf themes owned by organizations like Payments or Masterbrand.
Additionally, variants of these themes may be created to cater to specific use cases.
These developments will provide more options and flexibility for theming within Salt.
Salt is designed to be an extensible framework that enables teams to share common styling options, promoting design consistency.
It is important for Salt to cater to various LOB visual requirements while setting constraints to maximize adoption and avoid subjective aesthetic choices.

For example, to achieve "rounded corner buttons," we have implemented a solution that includes a single set of values catering to all existing visual options, such as mode and density, while supporting existing sharp aesthetics.
We have added the corner option with sharp as the default and rounded as an alternative, selecting values tailored for each density.
To ensure future extensibility, each option serves a specific responsibility.

For example, the "use Amplitude for heading text" option is specifically designed for heading text, and in the future, we may consider adding additional options for other text elements, such as display text.
It is also important to note that each option serves a specific business need.
For example, the JPM MasterBrand guideline specifies the use of teal as the primary color.
Therefore, we have designed an option to ensure consistent reflection of the accent color across all relevant components, while still maintaining the availability of blue accents.
These additions to the existing styling options (mode & density) enable Salt to support the adoption of Pepper users and existing Markets applications.

To ensure a smooth transition between different options, we would need the toggle to stay at a global level rather than at a per-component level.
This allows any styling switch to be applied globally (full page or application) or regionally (pattern reuse) instead of touching each component individually.
We also keep as many option mappings as possible at the

For example, variable modes can be set at a global level (page) or for a region (frame/section) to influence every component within each area.
As much as we want to isolate options, there are practical limitations.
For example, both accent and mode would impact color, so we can only offer "Mode & Accent" as a combined option using a single variable collection.
We won't be able to switch icon sets within components, which would require additional measures to overcome, such as a custom Figma plugin or, worst case, manual swapping.

Each product team could choose to use the default value or use some centrally managed preset.
By doing so, Salt will continue serving our community as the foundation and enabler, while enabling control and ownership for each team.
For example, the Pepper team could choose to align their product teams to use LD + Rounded + Teal.

We can also follow the Salt Business Pattern Index model, so that each team could publish their own preset, and those "crowd-sourced" presets can be picked by different team members through the Figma plugin without additional effort from th
We can leverage an npm package as a means of establishing consistency.
For example, the Pepper team can encapsulate preferred presets so that product teams can consume them without a deep knowledge of what options are available.
The Impact on Presets of Future Options

Taking this approach through code and design tooling means that if there are future requirements to extend the customizability of the system, such as providing a border/borderless switch, preset 'themes' aren't impacted.
At a base level, we can be opinionated as to what the default option is (bordered) and provide teams with the option to update their presets to include the alternative (borderless).
Until the option is added, the team/LOB would stay with whatever we set the default to.
Not every style option is suitable to be included within Salt.
If you want to deviate from the out-of-the-box (OOTB) styling, you should familiarize yourself with the available options to choose something as the baseline to build on top of.
Then use Salt design tokens to override the corresponding values, with an understanding of the increased maintenance cost in the longer run.
Salt is collaborating with the DXD Creative Tech team to provide better tooling to make this journey easier.
If your end goal is largely different from what Salt provides, then you can opt to create a net new theme.
To make this work, you need to supply values for each individual characteristics token.
It requires a deep understanding of the system as well as a significant amount of design effort.
However, you don't necessarily need to stick with any existing setup.
For example, you may choose to omit the palette layer altogether or not care about density.

title: 2025 Themes
content: As we continue to develop our components and scale the firm’s identity through Salt’s JPM Brand theme, we have seen an unprecedented breadth of adoption across the firm’s businesses.

Salt has replaced design systems across Corporate Technology and Global Banking–where it’s previously had no footprint–and continues discussions with delivery teams implementing AWM and CCB design languages.
With this growth, we recognize the need to evolve our brand theme so application teams can implement their design preferences.
Our consumers need to be able to stretch the brand theme to address the needs of application users, their workflows and their environments.
Salt’s objective is to enable delivery teams the capability to create more visual hierarchies through an extended choice of Salt styles to apply to components.

We primarily focus on understanding the visual styles required by consumers across businesses and prove a technical mechanism to implement the control of component and system styles in application builds.
It is important to note that Salt’s objective is to support a single JPM Brand theme that addresses the needs of businesses out-of-the-box (OOTB).
If delivery teams choose to create a
for Salt (i.e., to support a look-and-feel different to the firm’s brand) it becomes their responsibility to maintain.
To support extended styling of components, Salt:
Provides a default theme that aligns with the brand guidelines and can be used OOTB without additional complexity for consumers.
Includes an optional customization API that allows for supported change to specific visual attributes on either a per-component or system basis.
Adheres to semantic versioning (semver) of supported customizations so consumer preferences aren’t broken by updates.
Customizations will be strongly typed for a better Development Experience, reducing regressions and making tokens easier to use.
Customizations will be centralized, rather than applied per component, making it easy for delivery teams to maintain them.
Customization API will be independent of any third-party styling frameworks and compatible with custom, product-owned components.
Customization API will be user-friendly and intuitive, so users don't need to understand all the inner workings of Salt.
Customization API will be designed for high performance.
Salt will assess the correct mechanism to implement extended styling.

As technical proof of concepts (POCs) are tested for extended styling, Salt may update, remove and repurpose styling options to ensure the solution meets the mechanism requirements.
